m0-1.q: Aisyah's aunt says psychology is "just common sense about people". Which reply best reflects how psychology is actually defined?
opts: The scientific study of mind and behaviour
The study of mental illness and its medical cures
The study of the brain's anatomy and cells only
A set of personal opinions about people
m0-1.why: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behaviour (APA). It is not only about mental illness, not only about the brain, and it relies on systematic testing rather than opinion.

m0-2.q: A historian describes a man who, in 1879 in Leipzig, opened the first lab devoted to studying consciousness by training people to report their own experiences. Who is this?
m0-2.why: Wundt set up the first psychology lab at Leipzig in 1879 and used objective introspection. Titchener was his student who took the ideas to America.

m0-3.q: In an 1880s lab, a participant listens to a metronome and reports, as precisely and consistently as possible, the sensations and feelings it produces in her mind. Which method is she using?
m0-3.why: Objectively examining and measuring one's own thoughts and mental activity is Wundt's objective introspection. Free association is Freud's technique for reaching the unconscious.

m0-4.q: A researcher in America asks trained observers to break the experience of eating an orange into its sensations, images and feelings, to map the mind's basic building blocks. Which school does this reflect?
m0-4.why: Breaking experience into sensations, images and affections is Titchener's structuralism. Functionalism asks what the mind does to help us adapt, not what it is made of.

m0-5.q: A psychologist studies how students' attention and memory help them adapt to a new school, and suggests ways teachers could use this. Which early school fits this question best?
m0-5.why: Functionalism (William James) focuses on how the mind helps people adapt, live, work and play, and it influenced educational psychology. Structuralism would ask what the experience is made of.

m0-6.q: Jun Wei sees four separate dots arranged in a square and immediately perceives "a square", not four dots. Which early school would say this shows perception can't be understood by breaking it into parts?
m0-6.why: Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer) argued that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Structuralism did the opposite by breaking experience into elements.

m0-7.q: A patient has a paralysed arm with no physical cause. Her doctor believes a painful childhood memory has been pushed out of awareness and is causing the symptom. Which approach is the doctor using?
m0-7.why: Freud's psychoanalysis proposed that repressed urges in the unconscious cause nervous disorders and stressed early childhood. Behaviourism would ignore unobservable mental causes.

m0-8.q: A researcher refuses to study "thoughts" or "feelings" because they can't be directly seen, and records only what participants physically do. Which school does this match?
m0-8.why: Watson's behaviourism studies only observable, measurable behaviour. Structuralism relied on introspection about the mind, which behaviourists rejected.

m0-9.q: A baby is shown a white rat while a loud bang is made behind him, until he cries at the rat alone. He later fears other furry objects too. Which study is this, and what was it meant to show?
opts: Little Albert, showing that phobias can be learned
Pavlov's dogs, showing reflexes are inborn
Skinner's box, showing reinforcement shapes behaviour
Bobo doll, showing children copy aggression
m0-9.why: Watson's Little Albert study conditioned fear of a white rat to show phobias can be learned. It would be considered unethical today.

m0-10.q: A therapist explores how a client's sense of self developed and what hidden motives drive his relationships, drawing on Erikson rather than Freud's focus on sexual urges. Which perspective is this?
m0-10.why: The psychodynamic perspective is the modern form of psychoanalysis, focusing on the self and motives rather than sexual drives (Jung, Anna Freud, Erikson).

m0-11.q: A teacher gives a sticker every time a pupil hands in homework on time, and on-time homework increases. Which perspective best explains this change?
m0-11.why: Skinner's behavioural perspective explains voluntary behaviour as learned through reinforcement. The sticker reinforces handing homework in on time.

m0-12.q: A counsellor tells a client: "You are free to choose your path, and you have the potential to become the person you truly are." Which perspective does this reflect?
m0-12.why: The humanistic "third force" (Maslow, Rogers) stresses free will and self-actualisation. Behaviourism and psychoanalysis both see behaviour as more determined.

m0-13.q: A researcher studies how children's problem-solving changes as they grow and uses brain scans to see which areas activate when they reason. Which perspective is this?
m0-13.why: The cognitive perspective covers thinking, memory, problem solving and learning, including cognitive neuroscience and Piaget's theory.

m0-14.q: A study compares how students in Malaysia and the USA react when a teacher criticises them in front of the class, focusing on cultural norms about face. Which perspective is this?
m0-14.why: The sociocultural perspective looks at how culture and social settings shape behaviour, including cross-cultural research.

m0-15.q: A researcher tests whether a hormone imbalance in rats changes their aggression and checks whether similar effects appear in human patients. Which perspective is this?
m0-15.why: Explaining behaviour through biological events such as hormones, genes and nervous system activity, using animal and patient studies, is the biopsychological perspective.

m0-16.q: A psychologist argues that people everywhere fear snakes and heights because ancestors who avoided them were more likely to survive. Which perspective is this?
m0-16.why: The evolutionary perspective explains universal traits by their adaptive or survival value. Behaviourism would say the fears were learned in one's lifetime.

m0-17.q: Three psychologists explain the same teen's anxiety: one blames childhood conflict, one blames learned avoidance, one blames brain chemistry. What does this best illustrate?
opts: No single perspective explains all behaviour
Only one of them can be scientifically correct
Psychology has no agreed scientific method
Modern psychology has rejected older schools
m0-17.why: There are seven modern perspectives and none explains everything alone; each offers a different level of explanation of the same behaviour.

m0-18.q: Mei has severe depression. She needs both talk therapy and someone who can medically diagnose her and prescribe antidepressants. Which professional can prescribe?
opts: A clinical psychologist with a Ph.D.
A counsellor licensed by Lembaga Kaunselor
m0-18.why: Psychiatrists are medical doctors and can prescribe. Psychologists hold doctorates in psychology and typically do not prescribe; social workers focus on social and environmental support.

m0-19.q: Ravi wants to study how toddlers' language and social skills change from age 1 to age 5. Which area of specialisation fits best?
m0-19.why: Developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan. Clinical psychology focuses on diagnosing and treating disorders.

m0-20.q: A Malaysian counsellor is unsure whether a practice is allowed. Where should she look first for the standards she must follow?
opts: Her own country's professional body, such as Lembaga Kaunselor
The American Psychological Association only, since it is the biggest
Any guidelines she personally agrees with
m0-20.why: Practitioners follow their own country's guidelines; in Malaysia these include Lembaga Kaunselor and the Malaysian Society of Clinical Psychology.

m0-21.q: Two researchers measure stress in different ways and get conflicting results. They agree on one standard procedure, use objective measures and blind scoring. What are they trying to achieve?
opts: Reducing bias and error in measurement
Avoiding the need for ethical approval
m0-21.why: The scientific approach is a system of gathering data that reduces bias and measurement error.

m0-22.q: An Instagram post claims "Listening to Mozart raises IQ by 20 points!" Faiz checks who did the study, how big the sample was and whether it was replicated before believing it. What is he doing?
m0-22.why: Critical thinking means making reasoned judgments about claims rather than accepting them at face value.

m0-23.q: A researcher has already described a rise in students' exam anxiety and explained its cause. Now she designs a workshop to reduce it. Which goal of psychology is she pursuing?
opts: Prediction: when it will happen again
m0-23.why: The four goals are description, explanation, prediction and control. Designing a workshop to change anxiety is control.

m0-24.q: Hana notices classmates who sleep more seem to score higher. She states, "Students who sleep 8 hours will score higher than those who sleep 5." Which step of the scientific approach has she just completed?
m0-24.why: Noticing the pattern was perceiving the question; turning it into a testable prediction is forming a hypothesis. Testing comes next.

m0-25.q: A student asks why modern psychology insists on research ethics when early researchers didn't. Which answer best fits?
opts: Harmful studies showed participants needed protection
Ethics rules mainly exist to slow research down
Older studies were all faked, so rules were added
Ethics only matter in medical research
m0-25.why: As research grew, harmful studies such as Little Albert showed the need to protect participants' rights and well-being.

m0-26.q: Before Siti can run her survey on self-harm thoughts at HELP, a panel of staff reviews her plan to judge whether it is safe for participants. What is this panel?
m0-26.why: IRBs, such as the HELP Ethics Review Board, review each proposed study for participant safety before it runs.

m0-27.q: Halfway through an experiment, a participant feels uncomfortable and wants to leave. The researcher says she must finish or lose her payment. Which ethical guideline is broken?
opts: Participants may withdraw at any time
m0-27.why: Participants have the right to withdraw at any time without penalty. Forcing her to continue breaks this guideline.

m0-28.q: A team wants to study the effects of destroying a small brain area on memory. Why might they use rats instead of humans, and what must they still ensure?
opts: It can't be done ethically with humans, but animals must not suffer unnecessarily
Rats are biologically identical to humans, so the results transfer exactly
Animal studies don't need any ethical approval at all
Most psychology studies use animals, so it is simply standard practice
m0-28.why: Animal research answers questions that can't be studied in humans, but animals must not suffer unnecessarily. Only about 7% of studies use animals.

n47.q: After a near-accident, Lim's heart pounds, he grips the wheel and shouts, and he thinks "I'm terrified". Which three parts of emotion does this show?
opts: Physical arousal, expressive behaviour and labelling the feeling
The id, the ego and the superego working together
n47.why: Emotion has three elements: physical arousal (pounding heart), behaviour that shows it (gripping, shouting) and inner awareness or labelling ("I'm terrified").

n48.q: Researchers show photos of happy, angry and fearful faces to a remote tribe with no contact with outsiders, and they label them the same way as students in KL. What does this support?
opts: Emotions are learned only from TV
Emotion words are identical in every language
The amygdala is larger in tribal groups
n48.why: Recognition of basic facial expressions across isolated cultures supports their universality.

n49.q: Asked how she feels after a breakup, a traditional Chinese-Malaysian student says "I feel dizzy", while her Westernised friend says "I feel sad". What does this illustrate?
opts: Emotion labelling is shaped by culture
Physical arousal is absent in some cultures
n49.why: Labelling is learned and shaped by language and culture. Tsai et al. (2004) found traditional Chinese Americans used bodily or social words, while Americanised groups used direct emotion words.

n50.q: Before giving a speech, Darren's heart races, he breathes fast and his pupils widen. Which system is producing this arousal?
n50.why: The sympathetic nervous system creates emotional arousal: faster heart rate and breathing and dilated pupils.

n51.q: A patient with damage to one brain structure can't recognise fear on others' faces and fails to learn to fear a tone paired with a shock. Which structure is damaged?
n51.why: The amygdala is linked to fear and identifying facial expressions, and is studied mainly through fear conditioning.

n52.q: Hiking, Aina jumps back from a curved shape before she realises it's only a stick, then calms down once she looks properly. Which explains the order of events?
opts: The fast low road reacted first, then the slower high road identified the stick
The slower high road reacted first, then the low road checked it
Only her cortex was involved, so she reacted after thinking
Her thalamus delayed the emotion until her body reacted
n52.why: The low road is fast, crude and subcortical, reacting before awareness. The high road through the cortex is slower and lets her recognise it is only a stick.

n53.q: Instead of dwelling on a bad grade, Nur reframes it as "useful feedback for the final", and her distress drops. Which brain region is most linked to this kind of regulation?
n53.why: Reappraisal, meaning reinterpreting a situation, is linked to the lateral orbitofrontal cortex. Distraction is linked to the anterior cingulate cortex.

n54.q: Ken explains: "I saw the bear, felt afraid, then my heart started racing, so I ran." Which view of emotion is this?
n54.why: Stimulus → emotion → physical reaction → behaviour is the common sense view. James-Lange reverses it: arousal comes first.

n55.q: Sara says: "I didn't feel scared until I noticed my legs shaking and my heart pounding; then I knew I was afraid." Which theory fits?
n55.why: James-Lange says bodily arousal comes first and is then interpreted as the emotion. Cannon-Bard says they happen at the same time.

n56.q: People with spinal cord injuries that cut off feedback from much of the body still report strong emotions. Which theory does this challenge most?
opts: James-Lange theory, because emotion should need bodily feedback
Cannon-Bard theory, because the thalamus is damaged
Facial feedback hypothesis, because faces are paralysed
Cognitive-mediational theory, because appraisal is lost
n56.why: James-Lange needs bodily arousal to be felt before emotion. Paralysed people and those with pure autonomic failure still feel emotion, which weakens it.

n57.q: Encik Lim says: "My heart started racing at the exact moment I felt afraid; neither came first." Which theory matches?
n57.why: Cannon-Bard says the thalamus signals the cortex and the sympathetic nervous system at the same time, so arousal and emotion are simultaneous.

n58.q: Participants hold a pen between their teeth (forcing a smile) while reading cartoons and rate them funnier than those holding it in their lips. Which idea does this support?
n58.why: Strack et al. (1988) showed facial muscle feedback can cause and intensify emotion: the more you smile, the happier you feel.

n59.q: After drinking strong coffee, Adam's heart races. He's at a party where everyone is laughing, so he decides he feels excited. Had he been in an argument, he'd have called it anger. Which theory fits?
n59.why: Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory says emotion needs both physical arousal and a label taken from environmental cues.

n60.q: Two students get the same B+. One thinks "I failed my goal" and feels sad; the other thinks "I improved!" and feels proud. Their bodies react only after this. Which theory fits?
n60.why: Lazarus says the stimulus is appraised first; the appraisal leads to the emotion and then the bodily response. Two-factor theory starts with arousal, not appraisal.

lt1.q: While choosing a gift, Mei pictures her friend's room, recalls what she likes and talks herself through options in her head. What is this mental activity?
lt1.why: Thinking is mental activity while processing information: organising, understanding and communicating it, often using words and images.

lt2.q: Asked "Which is a darker green, a lime or a frozen pea?", Jun answers by picturing both in his mind. What is he using?
lt2.why: Mental images are picture-like representations that let us inspect the properties of imagined objects.

lt3.q: Participants memorise a map of an island and mentally "travel" between landmarks. It takes longer to reach landmarks that are farther apart. What does this show?
opts: Mental images keep spatial properties like real pictures
Language controls how we think about space
Memories decay faster over long distances
lt3.why: Kosslyn's study showed scanning time increases with distance, so mental images preserve spatial properties.

lt4.q: Brain scans show that imagining an apple and actually seeing one activate similar lobes, but the visual cortex responds more strongly to the real apple. What does this show?
opts: They share brain areas, but perception is faster and activates visual cortex more
They use completely different brain areas with no overlap
Imagery activates the visual cortex more strongly than perception
Perception is top-down while imagery is bottom-up
lt4.why: Both activate frontal, temporal, parietal and occipital lobes; perception is faster, bottom-up and stronger, imagery slower and top-down.

lt5.q: A toddler who has only seen cats at home immediately calls a neighbour's new kitten a "cat". What lets him identify it?
lt5.why: A concept represents a category and contains key features, so new examples can be recognised.

lt6.q: A square must have four equal sides and four right angles. But deciding whether a raft counts as a "vehicle" depends on experience and is fuzzy. Which concept types are these?
opts: Square is formal; vehicle is natural
Square is natural; vehicle is formal
lt6.why: Formal concepts follow strict rules; natural concepts form from experience and have fuzzy boundaries.

lt7.q: Asked to name a fruit, most students in Malaysia say "durian" or "banana", while students in Canada say "apple". What explains this difference?
opts: Prototypes form from exposure to examples
Formal concepts have different rules in each country
lt7.why: A prototype is the example that best matches a concept, shaped by what a person is exposed to.

lt8.q: At a mamak, Aiman knows without thinking that he sits, orders, eats and then pays at the counter. What is this mental guide called?
lt8.why: Schemas are mental generalisations; scripts are schemas for familiar sequences of activities.

lt9.q: Lily must choose between three internship offers by listing pros and cons and picking one. What process is she mainly using?
lt9.why: Decision-making involves identifying, evaluating and choosing between alternatives; problem-solving is part of it.

lt10.q: To unlock a 3-digit combination lock, Danial tries 000, 001, 002 and so on through every possibility until it opens. Which strategy is this, and is success guaranteed?
opts: An algorithm, which guarantees a solution
Trial and error, which has no guarantee
A heuristic, which is a rule of thumb
Insight, which gives a sudden solution
lt10.why: Systematically checking every combination is an algorithm, which always finds the solution if one exists, though slowly. Random guessing would be trial and error.

lt11.q: Lost in a new mall, Siti heads for the escalators because "exits are usually near the escalators" — a rule that often works but isn't guaranteed. What is she using?
lt11.why: A heuristic is a rule of thumb based on experience that narrows down options but doesn't guarantee success.

lt12.q: After seeing news of plane crashes, Hana decides driving is safer than flying, though statistics show the opposite. Which heuristic is this?
lt12.why: The availability heuristic judges likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. Representativeness judges by how well something fits a category.

lt13.q: To write a thesis by May, Raj starts from the deadline and works back: final draft April, results March, data February. Which strategy is this?
lt13.why: Working backward starts from the goal and plans the steps in reverse. Subgoals break the goal into smaller parts.

lt14.q: After hours stuck on a coding bug, Kevin suddenly sees the solution while showering, realising it's like a problem he once solved. What is this?
lt14.why: Insight is the sudden "aha" perception of a solution, often when thinking of something else.

lt15.q: Needing a hammer, Faiz doesn't think of using the heavy shoe beside him because he only sees it as footwear. Which barrier is this?
lt15.why: Functional fixedness is seeing objects only in terms of their usual function. Mental set is sticking with methods that worked before.

lt16.q: Asked "How many uses for a paper clip can you think of?", Ana lists 30 creative ideas, while a maths test asks for the single correct answer. Which thinking does each require?
opts: Ana uses divergent thinking; the maths test needs convergent thinking
Ana uses convergent thinking; the maths test needs divergent thinking
lt16.why: Divergent thinking produces many ideas from one point; convergent thinking reaches one answer using logic.

lt17.q: To come up with ideas for her Creative Exhibition booth, Mei writes non-stop for 10 minutes without editing, then draws a mind map. What is she trying to do?
opts: Reach one correct answer through convergent thinking
Avoid functional fixedness by using a mental set
lt17.why: Brainstorming, journaling, freewriting and mind mapping encourage divergent thinking.

lt18.q: Using a limited set of words and rules, a child produces a sentence nobody has ever said before. Which property of language does this show?
opts: Symbols can be combined into unlimited new meaningful statements
Language is a fixed set of inborn calls
Language is exactly the same as any communication
Language is made only of sounds
lt18.why: Language is a system for combining symbols to make an unlimited number of meaningful statements for communication.

lt19.q: The word "unhappiness" can be split into "un", "happy" and "ness", each carrying meaning. What are these units?
lt19.why: Morphemes are the smallest units of meaning. Phonemes are the basic units of sound.

lt20.q: "The cat chased the mouse" and "The mouse was chased by the cat" have different word orders but the same meaning. Which aspects of language are being contrasted?
lt20.why: Syntax is the rules for combining words; semantics is meaning. These sentences differ in syntax but share semantics.

lt21.q: A father speaks to his baby in a high-pitched, sing-song voice: "Who's a good girl? Yes, you are! Good girl!" What is this called?
lt21.why: Child-directed speech is high-pitched, repetitive and sing-song, and creates learning opportunities for infants.

lt22.q: An 18-month-old says "Daddy go" and "Want milk", leaving out small words. Which stage is this?
lt22.why: Telegraphic speech (~1.5 years) uses short, simple sentences with only key words.

lt23.q: One theorist says a child must first understand the concept of "more" before learning the word; another says learning the word "more" helps form the concept. Who holds each view?
opts: Piaget: concepts first; Vygotsky: language first
Vygotsky: concepts first; Piaget: language first
lt23.why: Piaget argued concepts come before language; Vygotsky argued language shapes concept formation.

lt24.q: The Dani tribe have only two colour words, yet they perceive colours as accurately as English speakers. Which view does this support, and which does it challenge?
opts: Supports cognitive universalism; challenges linguistic relativity
Supports linguistic relativity; challenges cognitive universalism
lt24.why: Linguistic relativity (Sapir-Whorf) says language controls thought; the Dani findings support cognitive universalism instead.

lt25.q: Children told a bird is a "blackbird" assume it feeds its baby like another bird, even though it looks more like a bat. What does this study suggest?
opts: Category labels shape children's higher-level inferences
Appearance always beats labels for children
Young children can't form concepts at all
lt25.why: Gelman and Markman found labels guided children's inferences, suggesting linguistic relativity may affect higher-level concepts more than perception.

lt26.q: Kanzi the bonobo recognised about 150 words and followed some complex instructions, but never mastered grammar. What does this suggest?
opts: Animals can communicate, but there's no clear evidence they master syntax
Animals can learn full human language, including grammar
Animal communication is as deliberate and symbolic as human language
Kanzi's abilities prove the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis
lt26.why: Animals communicate, but there is no conclusive evidence they can master syntax; human language is voluntary and symbolic.

lt27.q: A blog claims bilingual people have far better executive function. A 2020 meta-analysis of many studies found something different. What did it find?
opts: Overall cognitive advantages of bilingualism are negligible
Bilinguals have much higher IQ than monolinguals
Bilingualism speeds up cognitive decline in old age
Bilinguals are worse at switching between tasks
lt27.why: Bilingualism was thought to boost executive function, but Gunnerud et al.'s meta-analysis found the overall advantages negligible.

sp1.q: Light hitting the eye's receptors is converted into electrical signals the brain can use. What is this conversion called?
sp1.why: Transduction turns outside stimuli into neural activity in sensory receptors.

sp2.q: In a lab, Ali detects a faint tone half the time it's played (A). Later he can just tell two tones apart half the time (B). Which thresholds are these?
opts: A: absolute threshold; B: just noticeable difference
A: just noticeable difference; B: absolute threshold
sp2.why: The absolute threshold is the lowest detectable stimulation 50% of the time; the JND is the smallest detectable difference 50% of the time.

sp3.q: Which of these is a classic example of the absolute threshold for taste?
opts: About 1 teaspoon of sugar in 2 gallons of water
One drop of perfume in a three-room apartment
sp3.why: The taste threshold is about 1 teaspoon of sugar in 2 gallons of water; the others are thresholds for sight, smell and hearing.

sp4.q: An ad flashes "Drink Cola" for 1 millisecond, too fast to notice consciously, hoping to influence viewers. What are these messages called?
sp4.why: Subliminal stimuli are below conscious awareness but strong enough to activate receptors; subliminal perception is their possible unconscious influence.

sp5.q: Ana stops noticing the classroom aircon hum (A), and her nose stops detecting her own perfume (B). Which is which?
opts: A is habituation; B is sensory adaptation
A is sensory adaptation; B is habituation
sp5.why: Habituation is the brain ignoring unchanging information; sensory adaptation is receptors becoming less responsive and sending fewer signals.

sp6.q: Two lights have the same wavelength, but one has a taller wave amplitude. How will they differ?
opts: The taller-amplitude light is a different colour
The taller-amplitude light is less saturated
sp6.why: Amplitude determines brightness; wavelength determines colour (hue); saturation is purity.

sp7.q: Light with a wavelength of about 700 nm is seen as what colour?
sp7.why: The visible spectrum runs from about 400 nm (violet) through 500 nm (blue) to about 700 nm (red).

sp8.q: In a dark room, which part of Mei's eye widens to let more light in?
sp8.why: The pupil is the opening in the iris; the iris muscles change its size with the amount of light.

sp9.q: Light passes through the eye to the layer at the back. Which cells convert light into neural signals, and whose axons form the optic nerve?
opts: Photoreceptors convert light; ganglion cells form the optic nerve
Ganglion cells convert light; photoreceptors form the optic nerve
Bipolar cells convert light; rods form the optic nerve
The lens converts light; cones form the optic nerve
sp9.why: In the retina, photoreceptors (rods and cones) transduce light, bipolar cells relay signals, and ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve.

sp10.q: Stargazing, Danial sees a faint star better by looking slightly to the side of it rather than directly at it. Why?
opts: Rods, which work in dim light, are concentrated in the periphery
Cones, which work in dim light, are concentrated in the periphery
The fovea has no receptors, so focus must shift away from it
Rods are concentrated in the fovea, so looking directly is worse
sp10.why: Rods are sensitive in low light and concentrated in the periphery; cones (colour, sharpness) cluster in the fovea and need bright light.

sp11.q: After a stroke in her LEFT visual cortex, a woman can't see objects in one part of her visual field. Which part?
sp11.why: The visual pathway is contralateral: the right visual field goes to the left visual cortex.

sp12.q: Every colour on a phone screen is made by mixing different amounts of red, green and blue light. Which theory of colour vision matches this?
sp12.why: Trichromatic theory says colour comes from the relative activity of three cone types (short, medium and long wavelength).

sp13.q: After staring at a green square for a minute and then looking at a white wall, Mei sees a red square. Which theory explains this afterimage?
sp13.why: Opponent-process theory (Hering) says red–green and blue–yellow are opponent pairs; fatiguing green lets red dominate.

sp14.q: Jason can't tell red apples from green leaves, but sees blue and yellow normally. Which type of colour deficiency does he likely have?
sp14.why: Protanopia (red cones) and deuteranopia (green cones) are dichromatic and cause red–green confusion; tritanopia affects blue–yellow.

sp15.q: A violin and a flute play the same note at the same volume, yet sound different. Which property of sound explains this?
sp15.why: Timbre comes from the purity or complexity of the sound wave; pitch comes from wavelength and volume from amplitude.

sp16.q: Loud concerts have damaged the tiny receptor cells in the snail-shaped part of Ali's inner ear. Which structures are affected?
opts: Hair cells in the organ of Corti
sp16.why: The cochlea is fluid-filled; its organ of Corti contains the hair cells, the hearing receptors that send signals along the auditory nerve.

sp17.q: Lin finds spicy and bitter foods far more intense than her friends do, and tests show she has many more taste buds. What explains this?
opts: More taste buds mean greater sensitivity to tastes
Taste buds are only on the tip of the tongue
Taste goes directly to the olfactory bulb
sp17.why: More taste buds make a person more sensitive; taste signals go to the gustatory cortex (anterior insula and frontal operculum).

sp18.q: A chef adds MSG to a soup to give it a rich, savoury taste. Which basic taste does MSG produce?
sp18.why: Umami comes from glutamate, as in MSG. Oleogustus, the taste of fatty acids, is a possible sixth taste.

sp19.q: Which sense sends its signals directly to the brain without first passing through the thalamus?
sp19.why: Olfactory signals go straight to the olfactory bulbs, bypassing the thalamus.

sp20.q: Holding a heavy bag, Amir feels deep pressure on his palm. Which skin receptor mainly detects this pressure?
sp20.why: Pacinian corpuscles detect pressure; Meissner's detect light touch; free nerve endings detect pain, touch and temperature; Ruffini endings detect pressure and stretch.

sp21.q: After bumping his knee, a boy rubs it hard and the pain feels less intense. Which theory explains this?
sp21.why: Gate-control theory says non-pain signals (rubbing) can close a gate in the spinal cord and reduce pain; endorphins also inhibit pain.

sp22.q: Two friends look at the same cloud: one sees a dragon, the other a rabbit. What process differs between them?
sp22.why: Both receive the same sensation, but perception, how sensations are interpreted and organised, differs.

sp23.q: Looking at Rubin's vase, Siti sees a vase, then two faces, and the image keeps switching. Which Gestalt principle is involved?
sp23.why: Figure-ground is the tendency to see objects against a background; reversible figures switch between the two.

sp24.q: Twelve dots are arranged in three tight clusters of four, and people see "three groups" rather than twelve dots. Which principle is this?
sp24.why: Proximity is perceiving objects that are close together as a group. Similarity groups things that look alike.

sp25.q: Looking at a logo with gaps in the outline, people still see a complete circle. Which Gestalt principle is this?
sp25.why: Closure is the tendency to complete incomplete figures.

sp26.q: A man who has lost sight in one eye can still judge depth fairly well in a photo or painting. Which cues allow this?
sp26.why: Monocular (pictorial) cues work with one eye; artists use them to show depth.

sp27.q: Standing on a straight railway track, Faiz sees the rails seem to meet in the distance. Which depth cue is this?
sp27.why: Linear perspective is when parallel lines appear to converge with distance.

sp28.q: On a train, nearby trees seem to rush past while distant mountains seem to move slowly. Which depth cue is this?
sp28.why: Motion parallax is when close objects seem to move faster than distant ones.

sp29.q: As a finger moves toward your nose, your eyes turn inward more and more and you feel the strain. Which depth cue is this?
sp29.why: Convergence is a muscular binocular cue: the eyes rotate inward more for closer objects. Binocular disparity is the difference between the two eyes' images.

sp30.q: Two equal lines look different lengths because one has arrow tips pointing in and the other has tips pointing out. Which illusion is this?
sp30.why: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, inward- or outward-turning ends distort perceived line length.

sp31.q: Told a photo shows a "ghost", students see a face in a blurry shadow; students told it's "curtains" don't. What explains this?
sp31.why: Perceptual set is the tendency to perceive things based on expectations or past experience.

sp32.q: Reading messy handwriting, Mei can't decode a letter alone, but reads the whole word using her knowledge of English. Which processing is this?
sp32.why: Top-down processing uses prior knowledge to organise features into a whole; bottom-up builds from the small features up.

l1.q: Which of these is an example of learning rather than maturation?
opts: A teenager learns to drive after weeks of lessons
A baby begins to walk at around 12 months
A boy's voice deepens at puberty
A child grows 5 cm taller over a summer
l1.why: Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour brought about by experience or practice. Walking, voice changes and growth come from maturation.

l2.q: While studying digestion, a Russian scientist noticed his dogs began drooling at the sound of the assistant's footsteps, before food arrived. Who was he, and what did he discover?
opts: Edward Thorndike; the law of effect
l2.why: Pavlov discovered classical conditioning through his work on digestion in dogs.

l3.q: After many visits, Aiman's mouth starts watering as soon as he sees the yellow sign of his favourite burger shop, before any food arrives. What type of learning is this?
opts: Classical conditioning: an involuntary response to a new stimulus
Operant conditioning: a voluntary response to consequences
l3.why: Classical conditioning is learning to make an involuntary response (salivating) to a stimulus other than the natural one (the sign instead of the food).

l4.q: When the doctor taps just below Mei's knee, her leg kicks out automatically, without any learning. What is this?
l4.why: A reflex is an unlearned, involuntary response.

l5.q: Before conditioning, a bell rings and Pavlov's dog simply turns its head; there is no drooling. In conditioning terms, what is the bell at this point?
l5.why: A neutral stimulus produces no reflex response at first; it becomes a CS only after pairing with the UCS.

l6.q: Whenever someone peels a lime in front of Aisyah, juice sprays into her eye and she blinks. Over time she blinks at the sight of a lime. What was the juice spray?
l6.why: The juice naturally causes blinking with no learning, so it is the UCS. The lime is the NS that becomes the CS.

l7.q: A patient on chemotherapy vomits every time she receives the drug. Later she starts feeling sick just walking into the hospital. What is vomiting in response to the drug?
l7.why: Vomiting to the drug is natural and unlearned, so it is the UCR. Feeling sick at the hospital is the CR.

l8.q: Students used to feel nothing when hearing the recess bell. After years of it signalling food, the bell now makes them hungry. What has the bell become?
l8.why: A neutral stimulus becomes a CS after being paired with the UCS (food), so it now triggers a learned response.

l9.q: Every time the dentist's drill whirs, pain follows. Now Jason's palms sweat and his heart races the moment he hears the drill. What is the sweating to the sound?
opts: A reflex to the drill's pain
l9.why: The sweating to the sound alone is a learned, reflex-like response to a CS, so it is a CR.

l10.q: Over two weeks, a trainer rings a bell just before giving a dog food, again and again, until the dog salivates at the bell. What is this phase called?
l10.why: Acquisition is the repeated pairing of the NS and UCS through which the learning is acquired.

l11.q: A researcher plays a tone AFTER giving food, and spaces them a minute apart. The dog never learns to salivate to the tone. What went wrong?
opts: The CS must come just before the UCS and close in time
The tone needed to be louder to act as a UCS
The dog also needed to be punished
l11.why: For classical conditioning, the CS should come before the UCS, close in time (seconds), paired many times, and be distinctive.

l12.q: A child bitten by a large German shepherd now fears all dogs, even small puppies. What explains the fear of puppies?
l12.why: Stimulus generalisation is responding to stimuli similar to the original CS. Hovland showed the response is larger the more similar the stimulus.

l13.q: A dog conditioned to salivate to a high tone at first drools to a low tone too, but the low tone is never followed by food. Soon it drools only to the high tone. What has happened?
l13.why: Discrimination is when the animal stops responding to a similar stimulus because it is never paired with the UCS.

l14.q: After conditioning, a dog hears the bell many times but never gets food, and its drooling gradually stops. What is this?
l14.why: Extinction is the weakening of the learned response when the UCS no longer follows the CS.

l15.q: A dog's drooling to the bell was extinguished last week. Today, after a rest, the bell rings and the dog drools a little again. What is this?
l15.why: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a learned response after extinction, showing learning is relatively permanent.

l16.q: A dog already salivates to a bell. The trainer now flashes a light before the bell, without food, and soon the dog salivates to the light alone. What is this?
l16.why: In higher-order conditioning, a strong CS (bell) is paired with a new neutral stimulus (light), which becomes a second CS.

l17.q: Rats get a shock at the start of a tone in one group and at the end in another. Only the first group fears the tone's onset. Rescorla says this is because the tone predicts the shock. Which view is this?
l17.why: Rescorla's cognitive view says conditioning works because the CS provides information that the UCS is coming.

l18.q: After a frightening car crash at a junction, Lin's heart races whenever she drives through any junction. What kind of learning is this?
l18.why: A CER is an emotional response classically conditioned to stimuli; it can develop into a phobia.

l19.q: Having never been stung herself, a girl becomes afraid of bees after watching her brother scream in pain from a bee sting. What is this?
l19.why: Vicarious conditioning is classically conditioning an emotion by watching someone else's reaction.

l20.q: A baby is shown a white rat while a steel bar is struck loudly behind him. Soon he cries at the rat alone, and later at a rabbit and a fur coat. What does the rabbit fear show?
l20.why: Watson conditioned Little Albert to fear a white rat; fear spreading to similar furry things is stimulus generalisation.

l21.q: After eating sushi once and then getting a stomach bug hours later, Kevin feels sick at just the smell of sushi. Why did it only take one experience?
l21.why: Conditioned taste aversion is a learned aversion to a taste followed by nausea, and it occurs after only one association, even with a long delay.

l22.q: Rats easily learn to avoid a taste linked with nausea after one pairing, but find it very hard to link a taste with electric shock. What explains this?
l22.why: Biological preparedness means animals learn some associations (taste and nausea) quickly because they aid survival.

l23.q: A shy student starts asking more questions in class because each time she does, the lecturer praises her. What type of learning is this?
l23.why: Operant conditioning is learning voluntary behaviour through its consequences; praise increases question-asking.

l24.q: A hungry cat in a puzzle box steps on a lever by accident and escapes to food. Over trials, it presses the lever faster and faster. Which principle explains this?
l24.why: Thorndike's law of effect says responses followed by pleasurable consequences tend to be repeated.

l25.q: A psychologist places a rat in a box where pressing a bar delivers food, and records only how often it presses, ignoring any "thoughts". Who designed this and named the type of learning?
l25.why: Skinner named operant conditioning and used the Skinner box, studying only observable behaviour.

l26.q: Every time Amir finishes his homework, his mother lets him play football, and he now finishes homework more often. What is the football?
l26.why: Reinforcement is any consequence that increases the probability of the response happening again.

l27.q: A coach rewards players with water on a hot day (A) and with team points that can later be swapped for snacks (B). Which is which?
opts: A is a primary reinforcer; B is a secondary reinforcer
A is a secondary reinforcer; B is a primary reinforcer
l27.why: Primary reinforcers meet biological needs (water); secondary reinforcers (points, praise, tokens) gain value through pairing with primary ones.

l28.q: A company gives staff a bonus for every month with zero safety accidents, and safe behaviour increases. Which consequence is this?
l28.why: Adding a pleasant stimulus (bonus) to increase behaviour is positive reinforcement.

l29.q: Siti buckles her seat belt as soon as she gets in the car because it makes the annoying beeping alarm stop. Which consequence keeps her buckling up?
l29.why: Removing an unpleasant stimulus (the beep) increases the behaviour, which is negative reinforcement. It is not punishment, because the behaviour increases.

l30.q: Two children get sweets for tidying: one every single time, one only sometimes. When sweets stop, which child keeps tidying longer, and why?
opts: The "sometimes" child, due to the partial reinforcement effect
The "every time" child, due to continuous reinforcement
Both stop at the same time
l30.why: Behaviour reinforced on a partial schedule is much more resistant to extinction than behaviour reinforced continuously.

l31.q: Staff work slowly at the start of each month and speed up just before payday, then slow again. Which schedule produces this pattern?
l31.why: On a fixed interval (payday), responding pauses after each reinforcement and rises as the time nears, giving a scalloped pattern.

l32.q: A boss checks emails at random times, sometimes twice in an hour, sometimes not for a day, so staff respond to emails at a steady pace all day. Which schedule is this?
l32.why: On a variable interval, the time before reinforcement varies unpredictably, giving steady responding with no pause.

l33.q: A coffee shop gives a free drink after every 9 purchases. Customers buy quickly toward the 9th, then pause after their free drink. Which schedule is this?
l33.why: A fixed ratio needs a set number of responses, giving a stair-step pattern with a pause after reinforcement.

l34.q: A gambler keeps feeding coins into a slot machine at a fast, steady pace because a win could come on any pull. Which schedule is this?
l34.why: A variable ratio rewards after an unpredictable number of responses, giving fast, steady responding that is very hard to extinguish.

l35.q: A dog trainer gives a treat 10 minutes after the dog sits, and also when it barks. The dog doesn't learn to sit. What should change?
opts: Give the treat immediately, and only for sitting
Give the treat less often, and for any behaviour
Give the treat before the dog sits
Punish the dog when it sits slowly
l35.why: Reinforcement works best right after the behaviour (especially for animals and young children) and only for the desired behaviour.

l36.q: Whenever a child grabs toys from classmates, she is sent to sit alone, and the grabbing becomes less frequent. What is being sent to sit alone?
l36.why: Punishment is any consequence that makes a response less likely to happen again.

l37.q: Driving without a seat belt, Faiz is stopped and given a saman (ticket). Which type of consequence is the saman?
opts: Positive punishment: adding an unpleasant stimulus
Negative punishment: removing a pleasant stimulus
l37.why: Adding something unpleasant (a ticket) to reduce behaviour is positive punishment.

l38.q: A teenager breaks curfew, so her parents take away her phone for a week. Which type of consequence is this?
l38.why: Removing something pleasant (the phone) to reduce behaviour is negative punishment.

l39.q: A father beats his son harshly for lying. The boy starts lying more skilfully, avoids his father and hits his younger brother. What do these outcomes show?
l39.why: Severe punishment can cause avoidance of the punisher, encourage lying, create fear and model aggression.

l40.q: A teacher wants to stop a pupil from shouting out answers. Which plan is most effective?
opts: Respond immediately and consistently, and praise hand-raising
Punish him occasionally, a few days later
Punish severely once, then ignore it
Punish only when she is in a bad mood
l40.why: Effective punishment is immediate, consistent and paired with reinforcement of the desired behaviour.

l41.q: Drivers speed up when they see a green light and stop at a red light. What is the light for the behaviour?
l41.why: A discriminative stimulus is a cue that a certain response will be reinforced.

l42.q: Parents decide to ignore their child's tantrums completely. The tantrums fade, but a month later one suddenly reappears. Which processes are shown?
l42.why: Ignoring removes the reinforcement (attention), producing extinction; the brief return later is spontaneous recovery.

l43.q: To teach a dolphin to jump through a hoop, a trainer first rewards it for swimming near the hoop, then for touching it, then for passing through it, then for jumping. What is this technique?
l43.why: Shaping reinforces small steps that get closer and closer to the desired complex behaviour.

l44.q: Raccoons trained to drop coins into a box for food keep "washing" the coins between their paws instead, despite losing rewards. What explains this?
l44.why: Instinctive drift is the tendency for trained behaviour to slip back to genetically controlled patterns, like raccoons' washing behaviour.

l45.q: A school uses rewards and consequences systematically to reduce bullying and increase cooperation among students. What general approach is this?
l45.why: Behaviour modification applies conditioning techniques to bring about desired behaviour changes.

l46.q: In a psychiatric ward, patients earn plastic chips for making their beds and attending therapy, which they swap for snacks or TV time. What is this system?
l46.why: A token economy rewards desired behaviour with tokens that can later be exchanged for reinforcers.

l47.q: When a 5-year-old hits his sister, he is sent to sit in a quiet corner for 5 minutes with no attention. What technique is this?
l47.why: Time-out is mild punishment by removal: it removes the chance of positive reinforcement through attention.

l48.q: A therapist teaches a child with autism to say "please" by rewarding small steps — eye contact, then a sound, then the full word. What is this modern approach called?
l48.why: ABA is a modern form of behaviour modification that uses shaping to build desired behaviour.

l49.q: A patient with high blood pressure watches a monitor showing her pressure in real time and learns to lower it by relaxing. What technique is this?
l49.why: Biofeedback gives information about biological conditions so that involuntary responses can be brought under voluntary control.

l50.q: A child with ADHD watches a screen showing his live EEG brainwaves and is rewarded when his attention-related activity increases. What technique is this?
l50.why: Neurofeedback is a form of biofeedback that uses EEG or fMRI to give feedback about brain activity.

l51.q: Which pair correctly contrasts operant with classical conditioning?
opts: Operant: voluntary and shaped by consequences; classical: involuntary and triggered by a prior stimulus
Operant: involuntary and triggered by a prior stimulus; classical: voluntary and shaped by consequences
Both: voluntary behaviours shaped only by consequences
Both: involuntary reflexes triggered only by prior stimuli
l51.why: Operant responses are voluntary (emitted) and depend on consequences; classical responses are involuntary (elicited) and depend on what comes before.

lp1.q: In the 1960s, psychologists argued that pure stimulus-response accounts can't explain how people plan, expect and understand, so mental events must be studied. Which approach grew from this?
lp1.why: Cognitive learning theories study the mental events behind learning, once psychologists realised cognition couldn't be ignored.

lp2.q: While driving, Aina mentally plans her route, recalls a road closure and expects heavy traffic, none of which is visible to observers. What are these?
lp2.why: Cognition refers to mental events occurring inside a person while behaving.

lp3.q: A psychologist runs three groups of rats through the same maze, giving food at different times, and shows that rats can learn without reward. Who is this?
lp3.why: Tolman and Honzik (1930) studied rats in mazes and showed latent learning.

lp4.q: Jamal rides as a passenger to college every day without paying attention to the route. When his friend is sick, he drives there perfectly the first time. What does this show?
lp4.why: Latent learning is learning that stays hidden until there is a reason to use it.

lp5.q: In a maze study, Group 1 is rewarded every day and Group 3 is never rewarded. Group 2 gets food only from Day 11, and its errors drop sharply the next day. Which experiment is this?
lp5.why: Tolman and Honzik used three rat groups with different reward timing to show latent learning.

lp6.q: Why is the sudden drop in Group 2's errors on Day 12 the key evidence in Tolman's maze study?
opts: They had already learned the maze without reward
Rats need shaping to learn mazes
lp6.why: Group 2's immediate improvement means they had learned the maze on Days 1–10 without reward; the learning was hidden (latent).

lp7.q: A chimp in a cage can't reach a banana. After sitting quietly, it suddenly stacks boxes and climbs up to grab it. Which researcher studied this, and what did he call it?
lp7.why: Köhler studied ape problem-solving and described insight learning.

lp8.q: Stuck on a puzzle for an hour, Lily takes a shower and suddenly sees how all the pieces fit: "Aha!" What kind of learning is this?
lp8.why: Insight is the sudden perception of relationships among the parts of a problem, the "aha" moment, not gradual trial and error.

lp9.q: A psychologist first noticed that dogs exposed to unavoidable shocks later stopped trying to escape, and later helped found positive psychology. Who is this?
lp9.why: Seligman, with Steven Maier, first observed learned helplessness and later helped develop positive psychology.

lp10.q: After failing every maths test despite trying hard, Ravi stops studying for maths at all, even when given a tutor who could help him pass. What explains this?
lp10.why: Learned helplessness is failing to act to escape a situation because of a history of repeated failures.

lp11.q: In Seligman's study, dogs in one group heard a tone followed by shock while held in a harness so they could not escape. What did the researchers expect them to learn?
opts: To fear the tone and escape it later
To feel relaxed when the tone played
To press a lever to turn off the tone
To copy the reactions of another dog
lp11.why: The assumption was that the restrained dogs would learn to fear the tone and escape it when given the chance.

lp12.q: In a two-sided box, dogs with no experience of inescapable shock quickly jump the hurdle to safety, but dogs that had been restrained lie down and whimper. What does this show?
opts: Latent learning of the box layout
lp12.why: Dogs that learned escape was impossible later failed to escape even when they could, which is learned helplessness.

lp13.q: A researcher shows children a film of an adult hitting an inflatable clown and later observes whether the children copy it. Who is the researcher?
lp13.why: Bandura studied observational learning with the Bobo doll experiment and proposed the learning/performance distinction.

lp14.q: After watching a YouTube video several times, Amira bakes a perfect cake on her first try. What type of learning is this?
lp14.why: Observational learning is learning new behaviour by watching a model perform it.

lp15.q: A boy watches his older brother swear but never swears himself, until a friend offers him RM5 to do it, and he swears exactly the same words. What does this show?
lp15.why: Learning can happen without being performed; the behaviour shows only when there is a reason, such as a reward.

lp16.q: Children who watched an adult kick and hit a Bobo doll later hit the doll themselves, while those who watched a calm adult did not. What does this show?
opts: Children can learn aggression by watching a model
Children were classically conditioned to fear Bobo
lp16.why: In the Bobo doll experiment, children who saw an aggressive model imitated the aggression.

lp17.q: Children who saw the model punished for hitting Bobo didn't hit it, until the experimenter offered rewards and they then copied the aggression perfectly. What does this show?
opts: They had learned it; punishment only reduced performance
They never learned the aggressive acts
lp17.why: Seeing the model punished lowered motivation to perform, but the learning had still occurred (learning vs performance).

lp18.q: For Danish to learn a dance by watching a video, he must notice the moves, remember them, be physically able to do them and want to. What are these?
opts: Bandura's four elements of observational learning
lp18.why: Bandura's four elements are attention, memory/retention, imitation/motoric reproduction and desire/motivation.

lp19.q: A child fails to copy a model's skill because she was busy playing with her phone during the demonstration. Which element of observational learning was missing?
lp19.why: The learner must first pay attention to the model; distinctive models help capture it.

lp20.q: Mei watches a cooking show attentively but forgets the steps by the time she reaches the kitchen. Which element failed?
lp20.why: The learner must retain the memory of what the model did.

lp21.q: A 4-year-old watches a professional skateboarder do a kickflip, remembers it and wants to try, but can't physically do it. Which element is missing?
lp21.why: The learner must be physically capable of reproducing the model's actions.

lp22.q: A teen sees a classmate get suspended for vaping and, though she knows exactly how to vape, decides not to. Which element explains why she doesn't copy it?
lp22.why: Motivation to imitate is low when models fail or are punished and high when rewards are expected.

mem1.q: A friend says memory works like a video camera that records everything exactly. Which description is more accurate?
opts: An active system that organises, alters, stores and retrieves information
A passive recording of everything exactly as it happened
A single brain area that stores all facts unchanged
A reflex that only responds to very strong stimuli
mem1.why: Memory is an active system that receives sensory information, organises and alters it while storing it, then retrieves it.

mem2.q: Aiman reads a phone number (1), holds it in mind for a minute (2), then later pulls it back up to dial (3). Which processes are these, in order?
mem2.why: Encoding converts input into a usable form, storage holds it, and retrieval gets it back out.

mem3.q: A textbook compares memory to a computer: input goes through sensory memory, then short-term, then long-term storage. Which model is this?
mem3.why: The information-processing model describes memory as three stages, like a computer handling data.

mem4.q: A researcher argues that when you recall "dog", many parts of a neural network activate at the same time — its sound, look, smell and feel — rather than one step at a time. Which model is this?
mem4.why: PDP says memory processes happen simultaneously across a large network of neural connections.

mem5.q: Group A counts the vowels in a list of words; Group B decides whether each word describes them. On a surprise test, B recalls far more. Which model explains this?
mem5.why: Processing by meaning (semantic) is deeper than processing by appearance or sound, so it is remembered better and longer.

mem6.q: For a split second after a camera flash, you still "see" the whole scene before it fades. Which memory stage is holding this raw information?
mem6.why: Sensory memory is the first stage, holding raw sensory information very briefly.

mem7.q: A grid of letters flashes for 50 ms. You feel you saw all of it, but it fades in about a quarter of a second, and a new image wipes it out. Which memory is this?
mem7.why: Iconic memory is visual sensory memory: large capacity, about 0.25 seconds, easily masked by new input.

mem8.q: Participants see a 3×4 letter grid briefly; a tone then signals one row to report, and they can recall most letters in any cued row. What does this show?
opts: The whole grid was briefly available in iconic memory
mem8.why: Sperling's partial-report method showed the whole grid is available in iconic memory, but only very briefly.

mem9.q: Your mum asks a question while you're scrolling. You say "What?" but then answer before she repeats it, because you can still "hear" her words. Which memory explains this?
mem9.why: Echoic memory briefly holds what was just heard for about 2–4 seconds, longer than iconic memory.

mem10.q: At a noisy party, you focus on your friend's voice but turn your head when someone across the room says your name. Which model explains noticing your name?
mem10.why: Treisman said unselected stimuli are attenuated (turned down), so important meaningful input such as your name can still get through.

mem11.q: Someone tells you a 6-digit OTP. You hold it in mind for about 20 seconds while typing it, but if someone talks to you, it's gone. Which memory stage is this?
mem11.why: STM holds information briefly (12–30 seconds without rehearsal) while it is used and is easily disrupted by interference.

mem12.q: Walking to the counter, Mei keeps repeating "teh tarik, two kaya toast, one half-boiled egg" in her head so she won't forget the order. What is she doing?
mem12.why: Maintenance rehearsal is repeating information in your head to keep it in STM.

mem13.q: Remembering the number 0123456789 is hard, but grouping it as "012-345-6789" makes it easy. Which concept explains this?
mem13.why: STM holds about 5–9 items; chunking groups bits into meaningful units so more fits.

mem14.q: While doing mental maths, Jun silently repeats numbers, pictures the column layout and decides which step to do next. Which model describes these parts?
opts: Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model
mem14.why: Working memory has a phonological loop (repeating numbers), a visuo-spatial sketchpad (picturing layout) and an episodic buffer, all controlled by the central executive (deciding steps).

mem15.q: You still remember your primary school best friend's name 15 years later. Which memory stage holds this?
mem15.why: LTM holds information more or less permanently, especially meaningful and important memories.

mem16.q: To learn the term "amygdala", Siti links it to her own fear of dogs and pictures an almond-shaped alarm. Her friend just repeats the word 30 times. Which method works better for LTM?
opts: Siti's elaborative rehearsal, because meaning adds retrieval cues
The friend's rote learning, because repetition is best
Neither, because terms can't enter LTM
mem16.why: Elaborative rehearsal makes information meaningful and adds retrieval cues, fitting the levels-of-processing model; rote repetition is weaker.

mem17.q: Ahmad can ride a bicycle smoothly but can't explain in words exactly how he balances. Which type of memory is this?
mem17.why: Nondeclarative memory covers skills, habits and conditioned responses; it isn't conscious but shows in behaviour.

mem18.q: On an exam, Lin consciously recalls that Wundt opened the first psychology lab, and also remembers sitting in that lecture. Which broad memory type covers both?
mem18.why: Declarative memory is conscious, known information: semantic (facts) and episodic (personal events).

mem19.q: Mei knows that Kuala Lumpur is the capital of Malaysia, but has no idea when or where she learned it. Which memory type is this?
mem19.why: Semantic memory is general knowledge such as facts and concepts, often without memory of when it was learned.

mem20.q: Lisa remembers exactly what she ate, who she sat with and what they joked about at her 18th birthday dinner. Which memory type is this?
mem20.why: Episodic memory holds personal events, such as what happened at a specific time and place.

mem21.q: When Ravi hears "hospital", he quickly thinks of "doctor", "nurse" and "medicine" rather than unrelated words. Which model explains this?
mem21.why: In the semantic network model, LTM is organised by meaning, and related concepts are stored close together and activate each other.

mem22.q: Hana can't remember a classmate's name until a friend says "she sat next to you in Bio and loved cats", and then it comes back. What did the friend provide?
mem22.why: A retrieval cue is a stimulus for remembering; the more cues stored with information, the easier retrieval is.

mem23.q: Divers who learned word lists underwater recalled them better underwater than on land. What does this show?
mem23.why: Memory improves when retrieval conditions match encoding conditions; here the physical place acted as a cue.

mem24.q: On an MCQ test, Aina picks the right answer easily, but in an essay with no options she can't produce the same term, though it feels "on the tip of my tongue". Why?
opts: Recognition gives more cues than recall
Recall gives more cues than recognition
mem24.why: Recognition matches information to a stored fact; recall must pull it out with few cues, so tip-of-the-tongue failures can happen.

mem25.q: After hearing a 15-item shopping list once, Tom remembers the first few and last few items best, but forgets the middle. What explains this?
mem25.why: The serial position effect means better memory for the start (primacy) and end (recency) of a list.

mem26.q: Without trying, Kim vividly remembers exactly where she was and what she was doing when she heard her grandmother had died. What is this?
mem26.why: Flashbulb memories are automatically encoded memories of unexpected events with strong emotional associations.

mem27.q: Each time Danial tells the story of his trip, small details change, influenced by photos he later saw. What does this show?
mem27.why: Memories are reconstructed during retrieval and can be revised by newer information.

mem28.q: After her team loses the final, Sara says, "I knew all along they would lose," though before the match she predicted a win. What is this?
mem28.why: Hindsight bias is falsely believing you could have predicted an outcome, because older memories are revised with new information.

mem29.q: After watching a crash video, witnesses asked how fast cars were going when they "smashed" (vs "hit") later recall broken glass that wasn't there. What is this?
mem29.why: Misleading information after an event (the word "smashed") alters the memory of it.

mem30.q: Students learn nonsense syllables; they forget a lot within the first hour, then forgetting slows down over the following days. Which finding is this?
mem30.why: Ebbinghaus found forgetting is fastest in the first hour after learning and then tapers off.

mem31.q: Two students study for 6 hours: one crams the night before; the other does 1 hour a day for 6 days. Who will likely recall more, and why?
opts: The spaced student, due to distributed practice
The crammer, due to massed practice
Both equally, since total hours are equal
The crammer, due to the recency effect
mem31.why: Distributed practice (spaced study) leads to better retrieval than massed practice (cramming).

mem32.q: You've seen thousands of RM1 coins but can't draw what's on the back. Why?
mem32.why: Encoding failure means the information was never put into memory to begin with.

mem33.q: A theory says memories fade because their physical trace in the brain weakens with disuse. Which fact is hardest for this theory to explain?
opts: Old memories returning after many unused years
Gradual forgetting of rarely used facts
mem33.why: Decay or disuse theory can't explain memories recalled after many years of not being used.

mem34.q: After switching to a new phone, Mei keeps typing her OLD PIN by mistake. Which type of interference is this?
mem34.why: In proactive interference, older information interferes with retrieving newer information. Retroactive is the reverse.

mem35.q: A patient can still play the piano perfectly but can't form new memories of facts or events. Which brain areas are likely intact and which damaged?
mem35.why: Procedural memories rely on the motor cortex and cerebellum; forming new semantic and episodic memories relies on the hippocampus.

mem36.q: Repeatedly practising a word list strengthens synapses so they respond more readily, with more and more sensitive receptor sites. What is this process?
mem36.why: Long-term potentiation strengthens synapses through repeated stimulation, supporting memory consolidation.

mem37.q: After surgery to remove his hippocampi to treat epilepsy, a man could still learn new motor skills but couldn't remember meeting his doctor minutes earlier. What does this case show?
opts: The hippocampus forms new declarative memories
mem37.why: H.M. couldn't form new declarative memories but kept nondeclarative learning, showing the hippocampus consolidates declarative memories.

mem38.q: After a head injury, Faiz can't remember the week before the accident, and he also can't remember anything new since. Which amnesias does he have?
mem38.why: Retrograde amnesia is loss of past memories; anterograde amnesia is inability to form new memories after the injury.

mem39.q: An elderly woman first starts forgetting recent conversations, and years later also forgets her children's names. Medication slows but does not stop it. Which condition fits?
mem39.why: Alzheimer's, the most common dementia, starts mainly with anterograde amnesia, later adds retrograde amnesia, and can be slowed but not reversed.

mem40.q: Most adults can't recall any events from before about age 3, even important ones. What explains this?
mem40.why: Infantile amnesia occurs because explicit memory depends on hippocampal changes and language, which develop later.

nc1.q: A Spanish scientist argued, against the view of his day, that the nervous system is made of separate individual cells rather than one continuous network. Who was he?
nc1.why: Ramón y Cajal (1852–1934) first theorised that nerve cells remain separate.

nc2.q: A car accident damages nerves in Hana's arm but not her brain or spinal cord. Which part of her nervous system is damaged?
nc2.why: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; the PNS is the nerves running through the rest of the body.

nc3.q: In a microscope image, one cell type carries electrical messages while the more numerous surrounding cells support, protect and nourish it. What are these two types?
nc3.why: Neurons receive and send messages; glial cells are the main support structures.

nc4.q: A toxin damages the part of a neuron that keeps the cell alive and holds its chromosomes. Which part is affected?
nc4.why: The soma maintains the cell's life, and the nucleus inside it contains the chromosomes.

nc5.q: A neuron's branch-like extensions are damaged, so it can no longer pick up messages from neighbouring neurons. Which part is damaged?
nc5.why: Dendrites receive messages from other neurons.

nc6.q: A neuron receives a message, but the signal never reaches the next cell because the long fibre from the cell body and its endings are damaged. Which parts are damaged?
nc6.why: The axon carries messages from the soma to the axon terminals, which communicate with other cells.

nc7.q: In multiple sclerosis, the fatty coating around axons breaks down and signals become slow and unreliable. Which structure is affected?
nc7.why: The myelin sheath insulates and protects axons and speeds up neural impulses.

nc8.q: Which part of a neuron forms the barrier that separates its inside from the fluid outside?
nc8.why: The cell membrane separates the inside of the cell from the outside environment.

nc9.q: When Aina touches a hot pan, which neuron first carries the "hot!" signal from her fingertip to the spinal cord?
nc9.why: Sensory, or afferent, neurons carry information from the senses to the CNS.

nc10.q: After the spinal cord processes the "hot!" signal, which neuron carries the command to Aina's arm muscles to pull back?
nc10.why: Motor, or efferent, neurons carry messages from the CNS to the muscles.

nc11.q: In a reflex, which neuron in the middle of the spinal cord connects the incoming sensory signal to the outgoing motor command?
nc11.why: Interneurons in the spinal cord link sensory and motor neurons; they also make up most neurons in the brain.

nc12.q: During an intense exam, a type of glial cell widens nearby blood vessels to bring more nutrients to active brain areas. Which glial cell is this?
nc12.why: Astrocytes control blood flow and dilate vessels during heightened activity, as well as synchronising axons and removing waste.

nc13.q: After a brain infection, a type of glial cell moves in to clear away viruses, fungi and dead debris, acting like the brain's immune system. Which cell is this?
nc13.why: Microglia remove waste and harmful microorganisms, working like an immune system.

nc14.q: A man recovers feeling after cutting a nerve in his finger, but a woman with damage to myelin in her spinal cord does not recover. What explains the difference?
opts: Schwann cells repair in the PNS; oligodendrocytes in the CNS often don't
Oligodendrocytes repair in the CNS; Schwann cells in the PNS often don't
Microglia rebuild myelin in fingers but not the spinal cord
Astrocytes build myelin in the PNS but not the CNS
nc14.why: Both build myelin, but Schwann cells in the PNS can reconnect and repair, while CNS oligodendrocytes are more likely to stay damaged.

nc15.q: In a developing embryo's brain, which glial cells act as scaffolding that guides neurons to their final positions, and later mostly become neurons themselves?
nc15.why: Radial glia guide neuron migration and axon and dendrite growth during early development; most later become neurons.

nc16.q: A drug blocks the use of ATP in neurons. Which process would fail, making it hard to restore the resting state?
nc16.why: The sodium-potassium pump needs ATP to push 3 sodium ions out and draw 2 potassium ions in.

nc17.q: Small molecules such as oxygen pass freely through a neuron's membrane, but sodium ions can only cross through special channels. What property of the membrane does this show?
nc17.why: A semipermeable membrane lets some molecules pass freely, while others need channels or pumps.

nc18.q: A neuron is not firing. Its inside measures −70 mV, with more potassium inside and more sodium outside, and its channels are closed. What state is this?
nc18.why: At resting potential the inside is negatively charged (−70 mV) and the sodium and potassium channels are closed.

nc19.q: For about one millisecond, the inside of an axon flips from negative to positive and back. What is this event?
nc19.why: An action potential is a brief reversal of the charge inside the axon, from negative to positive.

nc20.q: Put these in order: (A) potassium rushes out, (B) sodium rushes in, (C) the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting state, (D) a strong stimulus opens channels.
nc20.why: A strong stimulus opens channels; sodium rushes in (depolarisation); potassium rushes out (going past rest = hyperpolarisation); then the pump restores the resting potential.

nc21.q: At one moment a neuron's charge rises to +40 mV; shortly after, it drops to −80 mV, below its resting −70 mV. What are these two phases?
nc21.why: Depolarisation is sodium rushing in, making the neuron positive. Hyperpolarisation is potassium rushing out, so the charge goes below resting.

nc22.q: A weak touch slightly changes a neuron's charge, but no impulse fires. A slightly stronger touch triggers a massive depolarisation. What did the stronger touch reach?
nc22.why: An action potential fires only if stimulation reaches the threshold of excitement.

nc23.q: Like a gun that either fires fully or not at all, a neuron never fires a "half" impulse. Which principle is this?
nc23.why: An action potential fires at full strength or not at all.

nc24.q: Pressing gently versus hard on Mei's arm creates the same size action potentials in her neurons. How does her brain tell the pressures apart?
opts: By how often and how many neurons fire
It can't tell the pressures apart
nc24.why: Action potentials have equal intensity and speed; stimulus strength is coded by how often and how many neurons fire.

nc25.q: Right after firing, a neuron cannot fire again no matter how strong the stimulus; a moment later it can, but only with an extra-strong stimulus. What are these two periods?
nc25.why: In the absolute refractory period firing is impossible; in the relative refractory period a stronger-than-usual stimulus is needed.

nc26.q: Where on a neuron does the action potential begin?
nc26.why: The action potential begins at the axon hillock, a swelling where the axon exits the soma.

nc27.q: Sodium entering one point of an axon causes positive ions to spread along it, partly depolarising the next region until it reaches threshold and fires. What is this describing?
nc27.why: Positive ions flow to the next region, depolarise it to threshold and open its voltage-gated sodium channels, so the impulse travels along the axon.

nc28.q: Signals travel much faster along myelinated axons because the impulse leaps from gap to gap in the myelin. What is this called?
nc28.why: Nodes of Ranvier are unmyelinated gaps; the action potential is regenerated at each one and jumps between them (saltatory conduction).

n24.q: Feeling hungry, Amir gets off the sofa, walks to the kitchen and keeps searching the cupboards until he finds biscuits. What best describes this whole sequence?
n24.why: Motivation is the process by which activities are started, directed and continued to meet needs: getting up (started), going to the kitchen (directed), searching until he finds food (continued).

n25.q: Wei Ling hates running but trains every evening because her company pays RM500 to staff who finish the marathon. What type of motivation is this?
n25.why: She acts for an outcome outside herself (the money), so this is extrinsic motivation. Intrinsic motivation would be running because she enjoys it.

n26.q: Danial spends hours solving maths puzzles that nobody grades, simply because he finds working them out deeply satisfying. What is driving him?
n26.why: The act itself is rewarding, so this is intrinsic motivation.

n27.q: An early 1900s psychologist claims people collect things because of an inborn "acquisition" pattern and fight because of an aggression pattern. A critic replies that labelling a behaviour doesn't explain it. Which approach is criticised?
n27.why: McDougall's instinct approach listed innate patterns such as acquisition and aggression. Its weakness is that naming an instinct describes behaviour without explaining why it happens.

n28.q: After a long hike with no water, Kumar feels a strong, uncomfortable urge that pushes him to find a drink; once he drinks, the tension disappears. Which theory explains this best?
n28.why: Drive-reduction theory says needs create drives (tension) that push us to act to reduce that tension.

n29.q: Your body lacks water (A), so you feel tense and restless (B), which pushes you to drink. Which labels fit A and B?
opts: A is a need; B is a drive
A is a drive; B is a need
A is an incentive; B is an instinct
A is homeostasis; B is arousal
n29.why: A need is a requirement for survival (water); a drive is the tension and arousal that the need causes and that motivates action.

n30.q: Jessica works long hours because she wants money and her boss's approval; at lunch she eats because she is hungry. Which describes these drives?
opts: Money and approval are acquired; hunger is primary
Money is primary; hunger is acquired
n30.why: Primary drives meet survival needs such as hunger and thirst. Acquired (secondary) drives such as money and approval are learned through experience.

n31.q: When Aiman gets too cold he shivers, and when too hot he sweats, keeping his body temperature steady. Which concept explains this, and what is one limit of using it to explain motivation?
opts: Homeostasis; it can't explain eating dessert when not hungry
Homeostasis; it explains all motivated behaviour fully
Arousal theory; it can't explain shivering
Yerkes-Dodson law; it ignores body temperature
n31.why: Homeostasis is the body's tendency to keep a steady state. Drive reduction based on it can't explain eating when full or seeking extra arousal.

n32.q: Melissa always volunteers to lead group projects because she enjoys directing others and having influence over the final decisions. Which of McClelland's needs is strongest in her?
n32.why: nPow is the need for control or influence over others. nAch is about succeeding at challenging goals; nAff is about friendly relationships.

n33.q: After failing a test, Hafiz says, "I'm just not smart, and nothing I do will change that," and stops trying. According to Dweck, what does this reflect?
opts: A fixed view of intelligence and an external locus of control
A growth view of intelligence and an internal locus of control
