n33.why: Dweck links low achievement motivation to believing intelligence is fixed and outcomes are out of one's control. Believing ability can grow (internal locus) goes with high achievement motivation.

n34.q: Alex Honnold climbs huge cliffs without ropes, and scans show his amygdala barely reacts to frightening images. Which theory best explains why he seeks such extreme experiences?
n34.why: Arousal theory says people keep an optimal level of tension. Sensation seekers need more arousal; Honnold's low amygdala response fits this.

n35.q: Nadia performs a very difficult piano piece at a competition. According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, which level of arousal will most likely give her the best performance?
n35.why: Moderate arousal gives the best performance; for difficult tasks the ideal is on the lower side of moderate, while easy tasks benefit from higher-moderate arousal.

n36.q: Although she has just eaten, Rina buys a bubble tea because she walks past a shop advertising a new flavour with a free topping. Which approach best explains this?
n36.why: Incentives attract people into action independently of need or arousal. She wasn't hungry, so the external lure (pull) explains it.

n37.q: A refugee who lacks safe housing and regular meals is unlikely to focus on painting to express his full potential. Which theory explains this?
n37.why: In Maslow's hierarchy, lower deficiency needs (physiological, safety) must be met before higher growth needs such as self-actualisation.

n38.q: A manager lets staff choose how to do their tasks, gives them challenging projects they can master, and builds a close-knit team. According to Ryan and Deci, which needs is she supporting?
n38.why: Self-determination theory says a supportive social context meeting autonomy, competence and relatedness fosters intrinsic motivation.

n39.q: After eating nasi lemak, Mei's blood glucose rises; hours later, during a long exam with no food, it falls. Which hormones correct each change?
opts: Insulin lowers the high glucose; glucagon raises the low glucose
Glucagon lowers the high glucose; insulin raises the low glucose
n39.why: Both come from the pancreas: insulin reduces blood glucose and glucagon increases it.

n40.q: Mice lacking a certain hormone made by fat cells never feel full and keep eating until they become obese. Which hormone is missing?
n40.why: Leptin signals the hypothalamus that there is enough food, reducing appetite and increasing fullness.

n41.q: After damage to one area of its hypothalamus, a rat keeps eating far past normal and becomes extremely overweight. Which area was most likely damaged?
n41.why: The VMH may stop eating when glucose rises; damage causes overeating. LH damage does the opposite.

n42.q: A rat with a hypothalamic lesion refuses food and will only survive if force-fed. Which area was most likely damaged?
n42.why: The LH influences the start of eating; damage stops eating unless the animal is force-fed.

n43.q: Hui Min diets and loses 5 kg, but over the next year her weight slowly drifts back to where it was. Which concept best explains this?
n43.why: The set point is the weight level the body tries to maintain; metabolism and exercise can shift it.

n44.q: Two friends eat the same diet and do the same activity, but one burns far more calories just sitting still and finds it hard to gain weight. What differs between them?
n44.why: BMR is the rate the body burns energy at rest; a higher metabolic rate makes gaining weight harder.

n45.q: At 12:30pm Jason feels hungry even though he had a big breakfast, simply because everyone at the office heads to lunch then. Which factor is at work?
n45.why: Hunger is shaped by social cues and conventions (lunchtime), culture, preferences and food as comfort, not only by biology.

n46.q: A patient's BMI is 31. His doctor notes a family history of obesity, a stressful job and late-night fast food. Which statement fits?
opts: Obese, with heredity and lifestyle both likely contributing
Overweight but not obese, with only genes mattering
Obese, purely because of low willpower
A healthy weight, since BMI ignores metabolism
n46.why: WHO classes BMI ≥ 30 as obese. Obesity has many factors: heredity, hormones, overeating, food quality, lifestyle, stress and metabolism.

n61.q: A new employee quickly picks up company procedures from mistakes, learns the software and finds clever ways to fix problems with limited tools. Which concept is she showing?
n61.why: Intelligence is the ability to learn from experience, acquire knowledge and use resources effectively to adapt or solve problems.

n62.q: A school finds that students who score highly in maths also tend to score highly in languages, science and reasoning. Which theory does this pattern support most?
n62.why: Spearman's general factor (g) predicts that being strong in one area predicts strength overall.

n63.q: A teacher says one pupil is "musically gifted", another "bodily-kinaesthetically gifted", another "interpersonally gifted", treating each as a separate intelligence. A critic says these are talents, not intelligences. Which theory is being used?
n63.why: Gardner proposed nine separate intelligences. Critics (Hunt, 2001) say there is little evidence and that these are abilities rather than intelligence.

n64.q: When his car breaks down in a village, Farid has no idea how engines work, but he talks to locals, finds a mechanic and gets a cheap ride to town. Which of Sternberg's intelligences is he using?
n64.why: Practical intelligence is using information to get along and succeed in real life. Analytical is breaking problems into parts; creative is finding new solutions.

n65.q: A test report gives separate scores for processing speed, working memory, visual processing and reasoning, organised under broad abilities and an overall g. Which theory does this structure reflect?
n65.why: CHC combines Cattell's fluid and crystallised intelligence, Horn's added abilities and Carroll's three-tier hierarchy of cognitive abilities.

n66.q: At 70, Grandpa Tan beats everyone at vocabulary quizzes but struggles to work out a new phone game with no instructions. Which statement fits?
opts: His crystallised intelligence is strong; his fluid intelligence is weaker
His fluid intelligence is strong; his crystallised intelligence is weaker
n66.why: Crystallised intelligence is acquired knowledge, such as vocabulary; fluid intelligence is solving new, unfamiliar problems.

n67.q: Brain scans show that people scoring higher on reasoning tests have more efficient communication between frontal and parietal regions, plus strong working memory. Which theory does this support?
n67.why: P-FIT proposes that frontal and parietal areas, with some others, are key to intelligence, and links working memory to fluid intelligence.

n68.q: The French ministry of education asks for a test to find children who need extra help at school. A child who answers like a typical 6-year-old is actually 8. Who developed this test?
n68.why: Binet and Simon designed the first mental ability test for the French ministry to identify children needing remedial education.

n69.q: Most 10-year-olds can answer a certain set of questions, and 7-year-old Zara answers them all correctly. What is Zara's mental age?
n69.why: Mental age is the average age at which children can answer a given level of question, so Zara's mental age is 10.

n70.q: Using the Stanford-Binet formula, what is the IQ of a 10-year-old with a mental age of 12?
n70.why: IQ = mental age ÷ chronological age × 100 = 12 ÷ 10 × 100 = 120. This ratio method was used by Terman, building on Stern.

n71.q: A psychologist assesses a 9-year-old and reports an overall score plus five index scores: verbal comprehension, working memory, visual spatial, processing speed and fluid reasoning. Which test did she likely use?
n71.why: Wechsler tests (WAIS for adults, WISC for children, WPPSI for preschoolers) give an overall score plus five index scores.

n72.q: Students take the same IQ test twice, two weeks apart, and nearly everyone gets almost the same score both times. Which quality does this show?
n72.why: Reliability means a test gives consistent scores when given to the same people. Validity is about measuring the right thing.

n73.q: A "leadership test" gives very consistent scores, but they don't relate at all to how well people actually lead teams. What is the test lacking?
n73.why: Validity means the test measures what it is supposed to. Consistent scores show reliability, but here the test doesn't measure leadership.

n74.q: Before launching a new test in Malaysia, developers give it to 3,000 people of different ages, regions and backgrounds and use their scores as a comparison point. What is this process?
n74.why: Standardisation gives the test to a large representative group; their scores become the norms for comparison.

n75.q: On a test with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, Lina scores 130. What does this mean?
opts: She is two standard deviations above the mean
She is one standard deviation above the mean
n75.why: Deviation IQ uses mean 100 and SD of about 15, so 130 is two SDs above the mean (the gifted range).

n76.q: A rural child scores poorly on an IQ test full of questions about snow and baseball, but does well on Raven's matrices. What does this show?
opts: Cultural bias, and the value of culture-fair tests
n76.why: IQ tests can reflect the designer's culture. Culture-fair tests such as Raven's Progressive Matrices use non-verbal abstract reasoning to reduce this.

n77.q: After a motorbike accident, a doctor orders an IQ test for Hakim to check what cognitive damage occurred. Which use of IQ tests is this?
n77.why: IQ tests predict academic and job success and are used in neuropsychology to assess head injuries, learning disabilities and disorders.

n78.q: An 8-year-old has an IQ of 65 and cannot dress himself, manage money concepts or interact socially at the level of peers; this was noticed in early childhood. Which diagnosis fits best?
n78.why: Intellectual disability needs an IQ below 70, severe deficits in adaptive behaviour (conceptual, social, practical) and onset in the developmental period.

n79.q: A baby born to a mother who drank heavily during pregnancy has small facial features and later shows intellectual disability. Which cause does this illustrate?
opts: Fetal alcohol syndrome, an alcohol-related cause
A chromosome disorder such as Down syndrome
n79.why: Causes of intellectual disability include alcohol exposure in the womb (fetal alcohol syndrome), genetic disorders, deprivation, poor diet and toxins.

n80.q: A study follows children with IQs above 130 for decades and finds most became successful adults, but critics note the researcher was personally involved with them. Which study is this?
n80.why: Terman's study of gifted children (~2% with IQ 130+) found most became successful, but he lacked objectivity because he was too involved.

n81.q: Kelly notices her friend is quiet and upset, calms her own frustration before a group meeting, and uses her excitement to push through a hard assignment. What is she showing?
n81.why: Emotional intelligence is being aware of and managing your own emotions to reach goals, and understanding what others feel.

n82.q: Identical twins raised apart have more similar IQs than fraternal twins, who are more similar than adopted siblings. What does this pattern suggest?
opts: Twins share the same mental age
n82.why: IQ correlation rises with genetic relatedness; heritability is estimated at about 0.50, so environment matters too.

n83.q: Researchers notice that average raw scores on IQ tests in Malaysia have risen steadily over decades, so tests need re-norming. What is this called?
n83.why: The Flynn effect is the steady rise in IQ scores over time in modernising countries.

n84.q: Before a maths test, female students are told "this test shows gender differences". They score lower than women who weren't told. What explains this?
n84.why: Stereotype threat is when awareness of a negative stereotype about one's group lowers performance.

c1.q: Friends describe Jia Hui as calm, organised and kind, and she has been like this at home, at school and at work for years. What does this pattern describe?
c1.why: Personality is a person's unique and relatively stable way of thinking, feeling and behaving across situations and time.

c2.q: You can't remember your old house number right now, but you recall it instantly when asked. A painful memory, however, stays hidden even when you try. Which of Freud's levels hold each?
opts: The house number is preconscious; the painful memory is unconscious
The house number is unconscious; the memory is preconscious
c2.why: Freud's levels: conscious (current awareness), preconscious (easily retrieved) and unconscious (hidden, hard to access).

c3.q: A toddler screams for chocolate at the checkout and won't stop until he gets it, with no thought of consequences. Which part of personality is most in control?
c3.why: The id is innate, unconscious and impulsive, running on the pleasure principle: "if it feels good, do it".

c4.q: Starving during a lecture, Hannah wants to eat chips loudly but feels it would be rude, so she decides to wait 10 minutes for the break. Which part found this compromise?
c4.why: The ego is rational and acts as a referee between the id's urges and the superego's morals, following the reality principle.

c5.q: A cashier gives Raju too much change. Part of him wants to keep it, but another part insists "that would be stealing, it's wrong." Which part says it's wrong?
c5.why: The superego is the moral centre, built from learning society's rules, and contains the conscience.

c6.q: Leo spends his whole month's allowance on the first day because buying things feels good right now, ignoring that he'll have nothing left. Which principle is guiding him?
c6.why: The pleasure principle seeks immediate gratification with no regard for consequences.

c7.q: Desperate to sleep, Aina still waits until after her presentation to nap, because sleeping now would get her fired. Which principle is at work?
c7.why: The reality principle (ego) satisfies the id's demands only when it won't cause negative consequences.

c8.q: After lying to her mother about where she was, Mei can't sleep because she feels terrible about it. Which part of personality produces this feeling?
c8.why: The conscience, part of the superego, produces guilt after wrongdoing.

c9.q: Several people cope with exam stress in different ways, such as blaming the teacher, forgetting the exam date or acting as if it doesn't matter, without realising they are doing so. What are these?
c9.why: Defence mechanisms unconsciously distort reality to manage anxiety from conflict between the id, ego and superego.

c10.q: Despite three warning letters, Encik Rahman insists "My job isn't at risk, they're just being formal" and refuses to look for another job. Which defence mechanism is this?
c10.why: Denial is refusing to acknowledge a threatening situation. Rationalisation would be making up excuses for something already done.

c11.q: An adult who witnessed a car crash as a child has no memory of it at all, though relatives confirm she was there. Which defence mechanism might Freud say she used?
c11.why: Repression pushes threatening events out of conscious memory.

c12.q: After failing to get into a university, Kevin says, "I didn't really want to go there anyway, the campus is ugly." Which defence mechanism is this?
c12.why: Rationalisation makes up acceptable excuses for failures or unacceptable behaviour.

c13.q: Scolded by his boss, Ahmad says nothing, but goes home and shouts at his younger brother over a small mess. Which defence mechanism is this?
c13.why: Displacement redirects emotion onto a target that isn't the original cause.

c14.q: A teenager with strong aggressive urges joins a boxing club and channels them into training and competitions. Which defence mechanism is this?
c14.why: Sublimation turns socially unacceptable urges into socially acceptable behaviour. Displacement just moves the emotion onto an innocent target.

c15.q: A psychoanalyst says a client's adult habits come from being "stuck" because a childhood conflict linked to a body zone was never resolved. What is this idea called?
c15.why: Freud said personality develops through psychosexual stages centred on erogenous zones; unresolved conflict leads to fixation.

c16.q: A baby is weaned suddenly and harshly at eight months. According to Freud, which adult pattern is most likely?
opts: Chain smoking, nail biting or overeating
Seeing the opposite sex as awful
c16.why: Weaning is the oral-stage conflict (first 18 months); oral fixation shows as mouth-focused habits.

c17.q: Lisa's parents toilet-trained her very strictly. As an adult she is extremely neat, stubborn and stingy. Which stage would Freud say she is fixated at?
c17.why: Toilet training is the anal-stage conflict (18–36 months). Harsh training may produce an anal-retentive personality: neat, stubborn, stingy.

c18.q: A 4-year-old boy announces he wants to marry his mother and becomes jealous of his father. Which stage and complex does this reflect?
c18.why: In the phallic stage (3–6 years), sexual feelings awaken and the Oedipus (boys) or Electra (girls) complex appears.

c19.q: An 8-year-old girl says boys are "so gross" and spends all her energy on school, sports and friends of her own sex. Which stage is she in?
c19.why: In latency (6 years to puberty), sexual feelings are repressed and the child develops intellectually and socially, seeing the opposite sex as "awful".

c20.q: A 16-year-old begins dating and focuses romantic interest on others. Which stage would Freud place him in?
c20.why: The genital stage starts at puberty; sexual feelings can no longer be ignored and attraction focuses on others.

c21.q: A critic says: "Freud never ran experiments, his ideas can't be proven wrong, and he studied mostly wealthy Victorian women." What is she pointing out?
c21.why: Psychodynamic theory is criticised as unscientific, too ambiguous to falsify, and based on a narrow sample.

c22.q: A psychologist says Tom is shy because every time he spoke up as a child he was laughed at, so speaking up was punished and faded. Which view of personality is this?
c22.why: Behaviourists see personality as learned responses through conditioning; here shyness came from punishment (operant conditioning).

c23.q: After watching her older sister get praised for helping at home, Nisha starts helping too because she expects the same praise. Which view explains her behaviour?
c23.why: The social cognitive view says behaviour is shaped by observing others and by cognitive processes such as expectancies.

c24.q: A confident student speaks up more in class; teachers then call on her more, which boosts her confidence further and changes how she behaves. Which concept explains this loop?
c24.why: Bandura's reciprocal determinism says environment, behaviour and personal or cognitive factors all influence each other.

c25.q: Having aced past coding projects and been praised by mentors, Daniel is sure he can win the hackathon and works hard for it. Which concept explains his confidence?
c25.why: Self-efficacy (Bandura) is the expectation that one's efforts will succeed, built from past experience and perceived competence.

c26.q: Rotter predicts whether Alia will study tonight by asking how likely she thinks studying will pay off and how much she values a good grade. Which theory is this?
c26.why: Rotter said behaviour depends on expectancy (will it pay off?) and reinforcement value (how much do I want that outcome?).

c27.q: Hafiz keeps asking questions in class because he believes the lecturer will reward questions with participation marks. Which of Rotter's concepts is this?
c27.why: Expectancy is the belief that a particular behaviour will be followed by a reinforcing consequence.

c28.q: Offered either RM50 or a day off for finishing early, Jun chooses the day off because he values free time far more than money. Which concept is this?
c28.why: Reinforcement value is a person's preference for one reinforcer over others.

c29.q: After a poor exam, Siti says "I didn't revise enough, so next time I'll plan better," while Ali says "The lecturer just hates me." How do their loci of control differ?
opts: Siti is internal; Ali is external
Siti is external; Ali is internal
c29.why: An internal locus attributes outcomes to one's own actions; an external locus attributes them to fate or other people.

c30.q: Behaviour therapies are very effective for phobias, yet critics say behaviourists ignore what people think. What does this summarise?
opts: Evaluation of behavioural and social cognitive views
c30.why: Behavioural and social cognitive views are criticised for ignoring mental processes and overgeneralising, but they have produced effective therapies.

c31.q: A therapist focuses on her client's subjective feelings and his freedom to choose his own direction in life rather than on his childhood or conditioning. Which perspective is this?
c31.why: The humanistic perspective (Maslow, Rogers) focuses on what makes people uniquely human, such as subjective experience and free choice.

c32.q: Grace sees herself as "a caring, creative person who is bad at maths" — a picture built mostly from what parents and teachers told her growing up. What is this?
c32.why: Self-concept is the image of oneself, developed through interactions with significant people.

c33.q: After years in a stable job, Arif quits to pursue his lifelong dream of composing music, feeling he is finally becoming who he is meant to be. What is he striving for?
c33.why: Self-actualisation is striving for fulfilment and reaching one's full potential.

c34.q: Amy sees herself as average and lazy but believes she should be a top student and a leader. She feels constantly anxious. What explains her anxiety according to Rogers?
opts: A gap between her real self and ideal self
c34.why: Rogers said a big gap between the real self and ideal self leads to anxiety; a close match leads to feeling competent.

c35.q: Whatever grades Liyana brings home, her parents say, "We love you no matter what — let's see how we can help." What are they giving her?
c35.why: Unconditional positive regard is love and respect with no strings attached, which Rogers said is needed to explore one's potential.

c36.q: Ken's father only hugs him and says he's proud when Ken comes first in class; otherwise he is cold. What is Ken receiving?
c36.why: Conditional positive regard is given only when the provider's expectations are met.

c37.q: Raised with unconditional love, Nora trusts her own feelings, and the person she is closely matches the person she wants to be. How would Rogers describe her?
opts: Someone with an external locus of control
c37.why: A fully functioning person trusts their own feelings and has a real self that matches the ideal self, which requires unconditional positive regard.

c38.q: A student says: "Humanistic ideas sound lovely, but how do you test 'self-actualisation' scientifically? It's more philosophy than psychology." What is she pointing out?
opts: Criticisms of the social cognitive view
c38.why: Humanistic theory is criticised as idealistic, hard to test and more philosophical than psychological, though it inspired growth-focused therapies.

c39.q: An HR firm uses a questionnaire to describe applicants' characteristics and predict how they'll behave at work, without asking how those characteristics developed. Which approach is this?
c39.why: Trait theories aim to describe personality and predict behaviour, not explain where it came from.

c40.q: Whether at school, home or a party, Zul is consistently talkative and outgoing, year after year. What is this characteristic called?
c40.why: A trait is a consistent, enduring way of thinking, feeling or behaving.

c41.q: Two researchers go through an English dictionary and pull out words like "friendly" and "honest" to make the first list of personality traits, believing traits are wired into the nervous system. Who are they?
c41.why: Allport and Odbert produced the earliest trait list from the dictionary and believed (without evidence) that traits are wired into the nervous system.

c42.q: At a party, others notice that Wen is quiet and avoids big crowds. According to Cattell, what are these easily observed characteristics?
c42.why: Surface traits are characteristics easily seen by others; they come from deeper source traits.

c43.q: Cattell argues that Wen's quietness, shyness and dislike of crowds all stem from one deeper underlying trait, introversion. What is introversion here?
c43.why: Source traits are the basic traits underlying surface traits and form the core of personality.

c44.q: A psychologist gives a questionnaire measuring 16 traits, each scored on a dimension between two opposite ends, such as reserved vs warm. Which test is this?
c44.why: The 16PF measures Cattell's 16 source traits, each a dimension with two opposite ends.

c45.q: A personality report rates Hana high on openness and agreeableness, average on extraversion, and low on neuroticism. Which model is used?
c45.why: OCEAN (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism) is the Big Five.

c46.q: Faisal, a strong extravert, cracks jokes at a birthday party but stays quiet and respectful at a funeral. What does this illustrate?
opts: A change in his source traits
c46.why: The situation influences how a trait is expressed, so his extraversion shows differently by context.

c47.q: Researchers find the same five personality dimensions in Malaysia, Brazil and Germany, across languages, and self-ratings match friends' ratings. What does this support?
opts: The Big Five is largely consistent across cultures
Personality is entirely learned from culture
Only Western cultures have the Big Five
c47.why: Big Five factors appear across major cultural regions and languages, with matching self and observer ratings, though some regional variation exists.

n1.q: Dog breeders find that puppies of calm breeds stay calm even when raised by owners of aggressive breeds. Which field would study this as evidence about personality?
n1.why: Behavioural genetics studies the genetic bases of personality, using evidence such as animal breeding and twin and adoption studies.

n2.q: Adopted children's shyness matches their biological parents' shyness more than their adoptive parents'. What does this suggest?
opts: Personality is entirely learned at home
Adoptive parents have no influence at all
n2.why: Twin and adoption studies suggest genes contribute substantially to traits such as shyness and aggressiveness.

n3.q: Identical twins separated at birth are reunited at 39 and discover they both married a Linda, then a Betty, and share hobbies and habits. What is this famous case used to suggest?
n3.why: The "Jim" twins, raised apart, showed striking similarities, suggesting genetics plays a big role in personality.

n4.q: In 1796, a doctor feels a man's skull, finds a bump above his ear and declares him "highly secretive". Which discredited idea is this?
n4.why: Franz Joseph Gall's phrenology claimed personality could be read from the shape of the skull.

n5.q: An MRI study links higher extraversion to greater volume in the medial orbitofrontal cortex, a reward-value area. Which study is this?
n5.why: DeYoung et al. (2010) linked Big Five traits to brain-area volume, e.g. extraversion with reward-related regions.

n6.q: A textbook says about 50% of the variation in the Big Five traits in a population is due to genetics. What is this figure called?
n6.why: Heritability is how much of a trait's variation in a population is due to genetics; for the Big Five it is about 50%.

n7.q: In one country people value duty, tradition, respect for elders and group harmony; in another they value autonomy, change and personal achievement. Which dimension differs?
n7.why: Hofstede: collectivistic cultures value duty, order and the group; individualistic cultures value autonomy and individual security.

n8.q: In a company, junior staff never question the CEO's decisions and expect that power naturally sits with a few at the top. Which of Hofstede's dimensions is high here?
n8.why: Power distance is how much less powerful members accept and expect power to be held by a few.

n9.q: In one culture, both men and women are expected to be modest and caring rather than competitive and assertive. How would Hofstede classify it?
n9.why: Feminine cultures value modesty and caring for both sexes; masculine cultures value assertiveness and competition, especially for men.

n10.q: A country has strict rules for everything, many safety regulations and a strong belief in one right way. Which of Hofstede's dimensions is high?
n10.why: High uncertainty avoidance means low tolerance for ambiguity: strict rules, many safety measures and a belief in one truth.

n11.q: A clinical psychologist uses a structured interview, a trait inventory and an observation checklist, choosing parts of different theories to fit her client. What approach is this?
n11.why: Eclectic assessment picks parts of different theories to suit the situation and purpose.

n12.q: A school counsellor wants to assess a student's personality using a story-telling task with ambiguous pictures. Which category of assessment is this?
n12.why: The four types are interviews, behavioural assessments, inventories and projective tests. Telling stories about ambiguous pictures (TAT) is projective.

n13.q: A counsellor asks a client set questions about her worries, then follows up on whatever she raises. But because the client is charming, the counsellor rates her more positively overall. Which method is used, and which limitation appears?
n13.why: Interviews can be unstructured or semi-structured. A limitation is the halo effect, where one positive impression colours the whole judgement.

n14.q: A psychologist sits in a classroom and counts how many times a child leaves his seat in 30 minutes. The child behaves better because he knows he is watched. Which method and limitation is this?
n14.why: Frequency counts are a behavioural assessment. The observer effect means people behave differently when watched.

n15.q: Job applicants answer 100 true/false statements about themselves on a computer, and every answer is scored the same way. What kind of assessment is this?
n15.why: Personality inventories are standardised self-report questionnaires with fixed answer formats, often used by trait theorists.

n16.q: A forensic psychologist needs to check for psychopathology and whether a defendant is faking symptoms, using 335 statements with validity scales. Which test fits?
n16.why: The MMPI-3 assesses abnormal behaviour and psychopathology and has validity scales for over- and under-reporting.

n17.q: A researcher needs a detailed 240-item measure of the five main personality dimensions for a study on openness and creativity. Which test fits?
n17.why: The NEO-PI-3 gives a detailed assessment of the Big Five (OCEAN) with 240 items.

n18.q: A career fair offers a test that sorts people into one of 16 types such as "INFJ", based on Jung's ideas. A psychologist warns it has limited reliability. Which test is it?
n18.why: The MBTI is based on Jung, has four dimensions and 16 types, and is popular for careers but has limited validity and reliability.

n19.q: A company likes a personality inventory because it is standardised and computer-scored, but worries applicants may answer in whatever way looks good. What does this summarise?
opts: Pros and cons of personality inventories
n19.why: Inventories are objective, standardised and more reliable, but people may give socially desirable answers or interpret items differently.

n20.q: A client looks at a vague, unclear image and is asked to say whatever comes to mind, on the idea that she will reveal hidden feelings. What type of test is this?
n20.why: Projective tests show ambiguous stimuli and ask for free responses, assuming people project inner conflicts onto them.

n21.q: A patient is shown 10 symmetrical blots and asked what each looks like; responses are scored on colour, shape and whether she uses the whole blot. Which test is this?
n21.why: Hermann Rorschach's test uses 10 inkblots, scored on colour, shape, figures seen and whole vs detail.

n22.q: A client is shown ambiguous pictures of people and asked to tell a story about what is happening and how it ends. Which test is this?
n22.why: The TAT (Henry Murray) uses ambiguous pictures; clients tell stories, and psychoanalysts look for projected problems.

n23.q: Two psychologists score the same Rorschach responses and reach very different conclusions about the client. What limitation does this show?
opts: Projective tests are subjective and unreliable
Interviews suffer from the halo effect
Observation suffers from the observer effect
n23.why: Projective tests are very subjective, lack standard grading and have poor reliability and validity.

sy1.q: Under an electron microscope, a researcher sees a tiny gap where the axon terminal of one neuron meets the dendrite of another, with chemicals crossing it. What is this junction?
sy1.why: A synapse is the site where impulses pass between nerve cells; neurons communicate by sending chemicals across it.

sy2.q: Neuron A releases neurotransmitter into the gap; Neuron B's receptors pick it up. Which is which?
opts: A is presynaptic; B is postsynaptic
A is postsynaptic; B is presynaptic
sy2.why: The presynaptic neuron delivers the transmission; the postsynaptic neuron receives it.

sy3.q: In 1906, a physiologist studying reflexes in dogs coined a word for the specialised gap between neurons. Who was he?
sy3.why: Sherrington coined "synapse" in 1906 based on his reflex studies in dogs.

sy4.q: Sherrington found that a reflex signal travels at about 15 m/s, but an axon conducts at about 40 m/s. What did he conclude from this delay?
opts: Something slows transmission at the synapse
Axons conduct more slowly than reflexes
sy4.why: Reflexes were slower than axon conduction, suggesting a delay at the synapse; his other findings (summation, muscle coordination) also pointed to special synaptic processes.

sy5.q: A single light pinch on a dog's foot causes no reflex, but three quick pinches on the same spot, a split second apart, trigger a leg withdrawal. What explains this?
sy5.why: Temporal summation is when repeated stimuli over a short time add up to trigger an impulse that one weak stimulus can't.

sy6.q: One light touch on a dog's foot does nothing, but three light touches at the same moment on three nearby spots trigger a reflex. What explains this?
sy6.why: Spatial summation is input from several locations adding up to trigger an impulse.

sy7.q: Glutamate opens channels that let positive sodium ions into a postsynaptic neuron, nudging it closer to firing. What is this small change called?
sy7.why: An EPSP is a graded depolarisation from positive ions flowing in, making an action potential more likely.

sy8.q: GABA opens chloride channels, letting negative ions into the postsynaptic cell and making it less likely to fire. What is this?
sy8.why: An IPSP is temporary hyperpolarisation, from potassium leaving or chloride entering, acting as a brake on excitation.

sy9.q: A neuron receives 300 excitatory and 400 inhibitory inputs at once. What decides whether it fires?
opts: The balance of EPSPs and IPSPs
sy9.why: Whether an action potential fires depends on the ratio of IPSPs to EPSPs summed at that moment.

sy10.q: A scientist stimulates a frog heart's vagus nerve, slowing it, then moves fluid from around it to a second heart, which also slows. What did this prove?
sy10.why: Loewi showed that stimulating a nerve releases chemicals that alter the next cell, proving chemical transmission.

sy11.q: What are the chemicals that cross the synaptic gap to let one neuron influence the next?
sy11.why: Neurotransmitters travel across the synapse to allow communication; chemical transmission was accepted as the main type around 1950.

sy12.q: A neuron makes a neurotransmitter and keeps it packed in tiny sacs inside its axon terminal until needed. What are these sacs?
sy12.why: Neurotransmitters are synthesised and stored in synaptic vesicles in the presynaptic terminal.

sy13.q: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, calcium enters and vesicles release their contents into the synaptic cleft. What is this release called?
sy13.why: Calcium entry triggers exocytosis: neurotransmitter is expelled from the presynaptic terminal into the cleft.

sy14.q: Serotonin crosses the cleft and binds only to proteins on the next neuron's dendrite that are shaped to fit it, like a key in a lock. What are these proteins?
sy14.why: Receptor sites are proteins shaped to fit only certain neurotransmitters.

sy15.q: After signalling, some serotonin is pumped back into the presynaptic neuron, while some is broken down by monoamine oxidase. Which two processes are these?
sy15.why: Reuptake takes neurotransmitter back into the presynaptic neuron; enzymatic degradation (e.g. by MAO) alters it so it can't act.

sy16.q: A drug that blocks one neurotransmitter causes muscle weakness and also impairs memory, since the same chemical works in the hippocampus. Which neurotransmitter is blocked?
sy16.why: Acetylcholine controls muscle contractions and also plays a role in memory, attention and arousal.

sy17.q: A man develops tremors and difficulty starting movements because neurons in one brain area produce too little of a neurotransmitter. Which disease and chemical?
sy17.why: Too little dopamine in certain areas causes Parkinson's; too much in other areas is linked to schizophrenia.

sy18.q: A drug strongly increases the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, making people sleepy and calm and slowing movement. Which neurotransmitter is it?
sy18.why: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter, involved in sleep and inhibiting movement. Glutamate is the major excitatory one.

sy19.q: Valium (a benzodiazepine) boosts GABA's calming effect at its receptors, while an antipsychotic blocks dopamine receptors. What is each drug?
opts: Benzodiazepine is a GABA agonist; antipsychotic is a dopamine antagonist
Benzodiazepine is an antagonist; antipsychotic is an agonist
sy19.why: Agonists mimic or enhance a neurotransmitter's effect; antagonists block or reduce it.

sy20.q: An antidepressant keeps more serotonin in the synapse by stopping it being taken back into the presynaptic neuron. Which drug type is this?
sy20.why: SSRIs block reuptake of serotonin. MAOIs block the enzyme that breaks down neurotransmitters.

sy21.q: Two neurotransmitters bind to postsynaptic receptors: one opens sodium channels, the other opens chloride channels. What decides whether each produces an EPSP or an IPSP?
opts: Which ion channel the receptor opens
The size of the presynaptic neuron
sy21.why: Receptor activation opens ion channels; which ions flow decides whether the result is an EPSP or IPSP. The receptor type (ionotropic or metabotropic) also matters.

sy22.q: Visual signals must update in under a millisecond. Which receptor effect suits this, with ligand-gated channels opening immediately?
sy22.why: Ionotropic effects open ion channels instantly (< 1 ms) and are short-lived, suited to fast information such as vision.

sy23.q: Dopamine binds to a receptor, bending it and releasing a G-protein that raises a second messenger such as cyclic AMP, with effects lasting minutes. Which effect is this?
sy23.why: Metabotropic effects start a slower, longer-lasting chain via G-proteins and second messengers, suited to taste, smell and attention.

sy24.q: Before an exam, Aina's adrenal glands release a chemical into her blood that affects her heart, liver and muscles over many minutes. What type of chemical is this?
opts: A neurotransmitter acting only at one synapse
sy24.why: Hormones are secreted by glands into the blood and alter activity in distant organs, producing longer-lasting effects.

sy25.q: A new mother's milk release and uterine contractions are triggered by one hormone, while jet lag disrupts her sleepiness hormone. Which hormones and glands are these?
sy25.why: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary causes contractions and milk release; melatonin from the pineal gland causes sleepiness.

sy26.q: When thyroid hormone levels rise too high, they signal the hypothalamus and pituitary to reduce the release that stimulates the thyroid. What is this mechanism?
sy26.why: Negative feedback is when a product feeds back to decrease its own production, restoring normal levels.

ns1.q: On a brain diagram, the cerebellum sits at the back and bottom, and the frontal lobe at the front and top. Which terms describe the cerebellum's position?
ns1.why: Posterior means towards the back and inferior towards the bottom; anterior and superior are front and top.

ns2.q: In a four-legged animal such as a rat, the nose end is ___ and the tail end is ___; the back is ___ and the belly is ___.
ns2.why: Rostral is towards the nose and caudal towards the tail; dorsal is towards the back and ventral towards the stomach.

ns3.q: A stroke in the left hemisphere paralyses the right arm. Relative to the damage, how is the right arm described?
ns3.why: Contralateral means the opposite side of the body; ipsilateral means the same side.

ns4.q: A neuroscientist cuts the brain down the middle, separating the left and right halves to show the corpus callosum. Which plane is this?
ns4.why: Sagittal slices separate left and right; coronal slices go front to back; horizontal slices go top to bottom.

ns5.q: A patient has nerve damage in his legs but his brain and spinal cord are healthy. Which system is affected, and what are its two parts?
opts: Peripheral nervous system: somatic and autonomic
Central nervous system: brain and spinal cord
Autonomic system: sympathetic and parasympathetic only
Somatic system: sensory and motor only
ns5.why: The PNS includes all nerves outside the brain and spinal cord and has somatic and autonomic divisions.

ns6.q: When you decide to kick a ball, the command travels from the CNS to your leg muscles. Which division controls this, and which pathway carries it?
ns6.why: The somatic NS controls voluntary muscles; the motor (efferent) pathway carries commands from the CNS to them.

ns7.q: Your heart rate, digestion and breathing adjust automatically without you thinking about them. Which division controls these?
ns7.why: The autonomic NS controls involuntary muscles, organs and glands, through sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

ns8.q: A deer spots a tiger: its heart races and digestion stops. Later, safely resting, its heart slows and digestion resumes. Which divisions act in each phase?
ns8.why: The sympathetic division prepares the body for fight-or-flight; the parasympathetic restores it for day-to-day functioning.

ns9.q: A knee-jerk reflex still works in a patient whose spinal cord is cut above the knee level, because the circuit is handled by cell bodies in the cord's centre. Which part handles the reflex?
opts: The grey matter of the spinal cord
The white matter of the spinal cord
ns9.why: Spinal grey matter (cell bodies and dendrites) handles reflexes; white matter (myelinated axons) carries information up and down.

ns10.q: A drug overdose depresses the lowest part of the brainstem, and the patient stops breathing. Which structure is affected?
ns10.why: The medulla controls life-sustaining functions such as breathing, swallowing and heart rate.

ns11.q: A brainstem structure that bridges the cerebellum to the rest of the brain and plays a role in sleep and dreaming is damaged. Which one?
ns11.why: The pons connects the cerebellum with the upper brain and is involved in sleep, dreaming and arousal.

ns12.q: After an injury to the network of neurons running through the middle of the medulla and pons, a patient struggles to stay alert and awake. Which structure is affected?
ns12.why: The reticular formation is responsible for attention, alertness and arousal.

ns13.q: A woman stumbles, has slurred speech and can't touch her nose smoothly with her finger after a stroke at the back of her brain. Which structure is damaged?
ns13.why: The cerebellum regulates balance, coordination and rapid movement; damage causes clumsiness and slurred speech.

ns14.q: A neurologist refers to the medulla, pons, midbrain and related structures together. What is this group called?
ns14.why: The hindbrain structures, midbrain and others together make up the brain stem.

ns15.q: An owl turns its head instantly toward a sound, while another animal quickly orients its eyes to a moving object. Which midbrain structures handle hearing and vision?
ns15.why: In the tectum, the superior colliculus handles vision and the inferior colliculus handles hearing.

ns16.q: Loss of dopamine-producing cells in a midbrain structure causes difficulty starting movements. Which structure is it?
ns16.why: The substantia nigra gives rise to the dopamine pathway that supports readiness to move.

ns17.q: Damage to the right cerebral hemisphere causes weakness on the left side of the body. Which part of the brain, and which principle, does this involve?
opts: The forebrain, which controls the contralateral side
The hindbrain, which controls the same side
The midbrain, which controls both sides
The spinal cord, which controls the opposite side
ns17.why: The forebrain's two hemispheres each control the opposite (contralateral) side of the body.

ns18.q: A set of linked structures around the brainstem, including the amygdala, hippocampus and hypothalamus, is studied for its role in emotion and memory. What is this system?
ns18.why: The limbic system includes the thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus, amygdala and cingulate cortex, involved in emotion, motivation, memory and learning.

ns19.q: After a small stroke, a patient loses some sight, hearing and touch, but her sense of smell is perfectly fine. Which structure was most likely damaged?
ns19.why: The thalamus relays most sensory information to the cortex, but smell bypasses it.

ns20.q: A tumour near the pituitary gland causes a patient to overheat, drink constantly and lose normal sleep-wake cycles. Which structure is affected?
ns20.why: The hypothalamus regulates temperature, eating, drinking, sleep-wake cycles and emotion, and controls the pituitary.

ns21.q: A patient can't form new memories of events (A), and another shows no fear when facing a snake (B). Which structures are damaged?
ns21.why: The hippocampus forms long-term declarative memories; the amygdala handles fear responses and fear memory.

ns22.q: A group of structures including the caudate nucleus, putamen and globus pallidus is damaged, causing problems with motor control and learning new movement routines. What are these structures?
ns22.why: The basal ganglia are mainly involved in motor control, plus motor learning and executive functions.

ns23.q: After a head knock, a doctor checks for a leak of the clear fluid that fills the brain's cavities and cushions it. What is this fluid, and where is it held?
ns23.why: The four ventricles and the central canal hold cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain and stores hormones and nutrients.

ns24.q: To stop severe seizures spreading, surgeons cut the thick band of fibres joining the two hemispheres. Which structure did they cut?
ns24.why: The corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres.

ns25.q: After a stroke at the back of her brain, a woman's eyes work perfectly, but she can't recognise or make sense of what she sees. Which lobe was affected?
ns25.why: The occipital lobe contains the primary visual cortex and the visual association cortex, which makes sense of visual input.

ns26.q: After damage at the top and back of his brain, a man can't feel touch on his hand or tell where his arm is without looking. Which area is damaged?
ns26.why: The parietal lobe's somatosensory cortex processes touch and body-position information.

ns27.q: A patient with damage behind her temples hears sounds but can't understand meaningful speech. Which lobe is affected?
ns27.why: The temporal lobe contains the auditory cortices and is involved in hearing and understanding meaningful speech.

ns28.q: After a stroke in the front of the brain, a man can't move his right arm voluntarily and struggles to plan his day. Which lobe and structure are involved?
opts: Frontal lobe, including the motor cortex
Parietal lobe, including the somatosensory cortex
ns28.why: The frontal lobe handles planning and decision-making, and its motor cortex sends commands to voluntary muscles.

ns29.q: After an iron rod pierced his skull, a once-polite railway foreman became impulsive, rude and unable to stick to plans. Which area was injured?
ns29.why: Phineas Gage's prefrontal injury caused personality change; the PFC controls executive functions and self-control.

ns30.q: One patient understands speech but speaks slowly in broken words (A). Another speaks fluently but produces meaningless sentences and can't understand others (B). Which areas are damaged?
opts: A: Broca's area; B: Wernicke's area
A: Wernicke's area; B: Broca's area
ns30.why: Broca's area (left frontal) supports fluent speech production; Wernicke's area (left temporal) supports understanding meaning.

ns31.q: A researcher passes a mild current through a wire into a rat's brain, making neurons fire, and watches the rat start eating. What technique is this?
ns31.why: ESB uses a mild current to activate neurons; lesioning uses a stronger current to destroy cells.

ns32.q: A Parkinson's patient has electrodes surgically implanted deep in his brain, connected to a generator in his chest. Which technique is this?
ns32.why: DBS is invasive, using implanted electrodes; TMS (magnetic pulses) and tDCS (weak current through the scalp) are noninvasive.

ns33.q: A patient with a metal plate in his skull needs a scan to check for a tumour. Which structural scan is suitable, and why not the other?
opts: CT, because MRI's magnet is unsafe with metal
MRI, because CT can't detect tumours
PET, because it shows structure best
EEG, because it has the best spatial detail
ns33.why: CT uses X-rays and is safe with metal; MRI uses strong magnets and gives more detailed images.

ns34.q: A researcher wants to know exactly when brain activity changes, to the millisecond, during a reaction-time task. Which technique is best?
opts: EEG, for its excellent temporal resolution
fMRI, for its excellent temporal resolution
ns34.why: EEG records electrical activity with good timing but poor spatial detail; fMRI and PET show where activity happens more clearly.
